title: Seeds: what a seed needs to sprout

summary.text: A dry moong seed can sit in a jar for a year without changing. On a wet cloth, it grows a white root in a day. Inside every seed is a tiny living plant with its own store of food. It sprouts when it gets water, warmth and air, even in the dark and without soil. Your child finds the baby plant in a soaked bean, then tests five cups of moong to find out what wakes a seed.
summary.art: A soaked rajma bean split open on a child's palm, showing the tiny baby plant tucked at one edge, with three small symbols floating above it: a water drop, a little sun for warmth and a swirl of air.

intro.hook: Hold a dry moong seed in your hand. It does not move, eat or grow. Is it alive? How could you find out?
intro.text: Look in your kitchen. There are jars full of seeds: moong, chana, rajma, methi, rai and jeera. They can sit in a jar for a whole year and never change. But put a few moong seeds on a wet cloth tonight. By tomorrow evening, most of them will have a little white root. What changed? What was the seed waiting for?
intro.art: A row of steel kitchen jars full of dal and seeds, and in front of them a wet cloth with moong seeds that have grown little white tails.

outcomes: I can name the parts of a seed: the seed coat, the baby plant and its food store.
I can say what a seed needs to sprout: water, warmth and air. I can say that most seeds do not need light or soil to start.
I can run a fair test with seeds, changing only one thing, and count how many seeds sprout.
I can show my results in a table and a bar chart, and work out how long sprouting took.
I can explain that a sprouting seed breathes, uses up its stored food and makes a little warmth.
I can describe how a seed sprouts: it drinks and swells, the root comes out first and grows down, and then the shoot grows up.
I can say what scientists agree on about seeds, and what they still do not know, such as how long a seed can stay alive.

terms.meaning: A baby plant packed inside a coat, with a store of food to start it off. Flowering plants and cone trees, like pines, make seeds so new plants can grow.
terms.example: Moong, chana, rajma, rice grains, rai and the stone inside a mango are all seeds.
terms.art: A line of seeds from a tiny rai grain to a big mango stone.

terms.meaning: The tough outer skin of a seed. It keeps the baby plant safe and dry until it is time to grow.
terms.example: The green skin on a whole moong seed is its seed coat.
terms.art: A moong seed with its green coat peeling off to show the yellow inside.

terms.meaning: The tiny living plant inside a seed. It already has a little root and a little shoot. Scientists call it the embryo.
terms.example: Split a soaked peanut. The small pointed part at one end is the baby plant.
terms.art: A split peanut with the tiny baby plant at its tip circled and magnified.

terms.meaning: The part of a seed that holds food for the baby plant. The baby plant lives on it until its first green leaves can make food from sunlight.
terms.example: The two big halves of a chana are its food store. That is also why chana feeds us.
terms.art: A chana split in two, the halves drawn as a lunch box with the baby plant sitting between them.

terms.meaning: The first leaves of a baby plant, already inside the seed. In beans and chana, they are thick and full of food. Scientists call them cotyledons.
terms.example: When a rajma bean sprouts, its two fat seed halves lift out of the soil and turn green. Those are its seed leaves. A chana's seed leaves stay under the soil.
terms.art: A bean seedling with two fat round seed leaves and two thin true leaves above them.

terms.meaning: A seed waking up and starting to grow. It is the scientists' word for sprouting.
terms.example: Moong left on a wet cloth for two days germinates. Each seed grows a little white root.
terms.art: Moong seeds on a cloth, day 0, day 1 and day 2, with the tails growing longer.

terms.meaning: A seed that has just started to grow, or the little root and shoot that come out of it.
terms.example: Moong sprouts in a salad, or in usal for breakfast.
terms.art: A bowl of moong sprouts with white tails.

terms.meaning: Alive, but resting. A dormant seed uses almost no energy while it waits for the right conditions.
terms.example: Rajma in a dry jar is dormant. It can wait for a year or more.
terms.art: A seed in a jar wearing a tiny sleeping cap.

terms.meaning: The part of a plant that grows down into the soil. It holds the plant in place and drinks water. It is the first thing to come out of a sprouting seed.
terms.example: The white tail on a moong sprout is its first root.
terms.art: A sprouted chana with a white root curving downwards.

terms.meaning: The part of a young plant that grows up towards the light. It becomes the stem and leaves.
terms.example: After the root, a green shoot comes out of a bean and grows upwards.
terms.art: A bean with its root going down and a hooked green shoot going up.

terms.meaning: To get bigger by soaking up water. Seeds swell when they are soaked.
terms.example: A cup of dry chana, soaked overnight, swells to fill about two cups.
terms.art: A small cup of dry chana beside a bigger cup of fat soaked chana.

terms.meaning: A gas in the air that living things need. Animals and plants use it to get energy from their food. Seeds need it too.
terms.example: You breathe in oxygen all day. A sprouting seed takes in oxygen too, very quietly.
terms.art: Tiny bubbles of air around a sprouting seed, one labelled 'oxygen'.

terms.meaning: How living things use oxygen to get energy from food. It makes a little warmth, and it gives out a gas called carbon dioxide. Scientists call it respiration.
terms.example: A heap of sprouting seeds gets warm because millions of its cells are breathing.
terms.art: A cloth bundle of sprouts with gentle warm squiggles rising from it.

terms.meaning: A kind of stored food made by plants. It is what makes rice, wheat and potatoes filling.
terms.example: Most of a rice grain is starch. The baby rice plant uses it to start growing.
terms.art: A rice grain cut open, its white inside labelled 'starch'.

terms.meaning: A helper made by living cells that speeds up a change. Some enzymes turn starch into sugar.
terms.example: Sprouted grains taste a little sweet, because enzymes have turned some starch into sugar.
terms.art: Tiny scissors cutting a long chain of beads into single beads, labelled 'starch into sugar'.

terms.meaning: A test where you change only one thing and keep everything else the same. Then you know what made the difference.
terms.example: To test if seeds need water, give one cup water and one cup none. Keep the cups in the same place, with the same seeds.
terms.art: Two identical cups side by side, one with a water drop symbol and one with a crossed-out drop.

terms.meaning: The force that pulls things towards the Earth.
terms.example: Gravity makes a dropped ball fall. Roots grow in the direction gravity pulls.
terms.art: A falling ball and a downward-curving root, each with an arrow pointing down.

terms.meaning: A safe store of many kinds of seeds, kept dry and cold so they stay alive for many years.
terms.example: Rahibai Popere, a farmer in Maharashtra, keeps a seed bank of old local crops. The Svalbard vault in Norway keeps seeds inside a frozen mountain.
terms.art: Shelves of labelled seed packets in a cool room.

explanations.definition: A seed is a baby plant inside a protective coat, packed with a store of food. It is made by a flowering plant, or by a cone-bearing tree like a pine.
explanations.description: Every seed has three main parts. The seed coat is the tough skin on the outside. Inside it is the baby plant, which scientists call the embryo. It already has a tiny root and a tiny shoot. The rest of the seed is the food store. It feeds the baby plant until its first green leaves can make food from sunlight.
examples: A soaked rajma bean: peel off the red coat, open the two halves, and find the tiny baby plant at one edge.
A peanut: the little pointed tip between the two halves is the baby plant.
A mango stone: the hard shell is the fruit's stone, and the seed with its coat is inside it.
explanations.art: A big labelled drawing of a split bean: the seed coat peeling away, the two fat halves of the food store, and the tiny baby plant with its root and two small folded leaves.
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea of the first half of the unit: what a seed is, and its three parts.

explanations.concept: Two kinds of food store: beans and grains
explanations.definition: In beans, chana and peanuts, the food is stored inside two thick seed leaves. In rice, wheat and maize, the food is stored in a separate part around the baby plant, and there is only one thin seed leaf.
explanations.description: Seed leaves are the first leaves of the baby plant, already inside the seed. Scientists call them cotyledons. A bean has two seed leaves. They are fat and full of food, so a bean splits neatly into two halves. A grain of rice or maize has only one thin seed leaf. Its food is kept in a separate store beside the baby plant. Scientists call that store the endosperm. When you eat a chapati or a bowl of rice, you are mostly eating the food store that a grain made for its baby plant.
examples: Chana and moong split into two halves. They have two seed leaves.
A soaked maize kernel does not split in two. Its baby plant is a small pale patch on one side.
Popcorn pops because water in the starchy food store turns to steam and bursts it open.
explanations.art: Side by side: a split chana showing two halves with the baby plant between, and a maize kernel cut open showing one pale baby plant beside a big white food store.
explanations.context: Not every seed is built the same way. This card compares the seeds of beans with the seeds of grains like rice and maize.

explanations.concept: What wakes a seed: water, warmth and air
explanations.definition: Germination is a seed waking up and starting to grow. Most seeds need three things to germinate: water, warmth and air.
explanations.description: Water comes first. It softens the coat and lets the cells inside start working again. Warmth matters because the changes inside a seed happen faster when it is warm. In a cold room, moong still sprouts, but slowly. In a fridge, it hardly starts. Air matters because the seed takes in oxygen, a gas in the air, to get energy from its food. Take away any one of the three, and most seeds do not sprout. In the five-cup test, the dry cup, the fridge cup and the cup under water do badly. The damp cup on the shelf sprouts, and the damp cup in the light does no better. The chart shows typical made-up results.
examples: Moong in a dry jar never sprouts. Moong on a wet cloth sprouts in a day or two.
Moong on a wet cloth in the fridge sprouts very slowly, or not at all, until it is warmed up.
Moong covered with water that was boiled and cooled, under a layer of oil, gets very little air. Only a few sprout.
explanations.art: Four cups in a row: a dry cup with sleeping seeds, a damp warm cup with sprouts, a damp cup with frost and a snowflake, and a cup full of water with a layer of oil on top and seeds lying still at the bottom.
explanations.context: This card answers the big question of the unit: what does a seed need to wake up? It uses results from the five-cup test.

chart.title: Made-up example: how many of 10 moong seeds sprouted in 3 days
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what typical results look like. Your numbers will be different.

explanations.concept: Most seeds do not need light or soil to start
explanations.definition: Most seeds can sprout in the dark, with no soil at all. They need light and soil only later, once the seedling must make its own food.
explanations.description: A seed carries its own food. So at the start it does not need sunlight to make food, and it does not need anything from the soil. That is why moong sprouts on a wet cloth inside a closed tiffin. Seeds in the ground sprout in the dark too. Light becomes important later, when the shoot comes up and its green leaves start making food. There are a few exceptions. Some small seeds, like some kinds of lettuce, need light to wake. In 1952, a team in the United States, including Harry Borthwick, Sterling Hendricks and Vivian Toole, showed that red light wakes these lettuce seeds, and a deeper red light, called far-red, stops them again. A small seed has only a little stored food. Light tells it that it is near the surface, so its food will not run out before the shoot reaches the light.
examples: Moong sprouts in a dark cupboard just as well as in a bright room.
Sprouts sold in markets are grown on wet sacks or trays, with no soil.
Some tiny seeds, like some kinds of lettuce, sprout only if light reaches them.
explanations.art: Moong sprouting happily inside a closed dark tiffin, beside a tiny lettuce seed with a beam of red light shining on it.
explanations.context: Many people think seeds need sunlight and soil to sprout. This card explains why most of them do not.

explanations.definition: A dry seed soaks up water and swells. This is the first step of germination.
explanations.description: A dry seed holds very little water, often only about one part in ten. When it gets wet, water rushes in. Most enters through a tiny hole next to the scar where the seed was joined to its pod. The scar is called the hilum. The seed swells to about twice its weight, and its coat goes wrinkly and then splits. Swelling seeds push very hard. A jar packed with dry chana and water can push its lid off. Once the cells inside are wet again, they switch back on and start to work.
examples: Weigh 50 grams of dry chana. Soak it overnight. It now weighs about 100 grams.
Soaked rajma has a wrinkly coat for a few hours, then it goes smooth and tight.
Look at a soaked bean. The pale scar on its side, the hilum, is where it was joined to its pod.
explanations.art: A bean seed in close-up with a pale oval scar on one side, little arrows of water flowing in through a tiny hole beside it, and the bean drawn twice: small and dry, then big and swollen.
explanations.context: What is the very first thing that happens when a seed starts to sprout? This card explains how it drinks and swells.

explanations.concept: A waking seed breathes and makes warmth
explanations.definition: A sprouting seed breathes. It takes in oxygen, uses it to get energy from its stored food, and gives out carbon dioxide and a little heat. Scientists call this respiration.
explanations.description: You breathe to get energy from your food. A seed does the same, without lungs. Every tiny cell in it takes in oxygen from the air around it. A dry seed breathes so slowly you could never notice. Once it is wet, it breathes many times faster. One sprouting seed makes too little heat to feel. But a big heap of sprouts, wrapped up, gets warm to the touch. A flask of live sprouts gets a few degrees warmer than a flask of boiled ones. That is also why a seed under water does badly. Water holds only a little oxygen, so the seed cannot breathe well.
examples: A cloth bundle of sprouting moong feels warm in the middle.
Farmers who sprout paddy seed in wet sacks before sowing can feel the heap warm up.
Seeds kept under water for too long go sour and slimy, because they could not breathe.
explanations.art: Two steel flasks with thermometers, the one with live sprouts showing a higher red line and soft warm squiggles, the one with boiled seeds showing a lower line.
explanations.context: Does a seed breathe? This card explains how a sprouting seed uses air, and why a heap of sprouts gets warm.

explanations.definition: As a seed sprouts, its cells make enzymes. These helpers break the stored food, such as starch, into sugar that the baby plant can use.
explanations.description: Starch is a store of food made of long chains. It keeps well, but the baby plant cannot use it straight away. When the seed wakes, enzymes cut the long chains into small bits of sugar. The sugar travels to the root and shoot, and feeds them as they grow. In grains like barley, the baby plant even sends a chemical message to the food store, telling it to start. In 1960, Leslie Paleg in Australia and Hiroshi Yomo in Japan each found this message. It is a plant hormone called gibberellin. This is also why sprouted grains taste a little sweet. People in India make ragi malt from sprouted ragi.
examples: Chew a two-day-old moong sprout slowly. Many people find it tastes a little sweeter than a soaked seed that has not sprouted.
Sprouted ragi is dried and ground to make ragi malt.
Malt for some sweets and drinks is made from sprouted barley.
explanations.art: Inside a sprouting grain: the baby plant sending a little envelope labelled 'message' to the food store, where tiny scissors cut long chains of starch beads into single sugar beads.
explanations.context: A seed carries a store of food. This card explains how the baby plant starts using it, and why sprouts can taste a little sweet.

explanations.definition: In most seeds the root comes out first and grows downwards. The shoot comes out next and grows upwards.
explanations.description: The root comes first so the seedling can hold on and drink. Whichever way up a seed lies, its root turns to grow down. Root tips feel gravity, the pull towards the Earth. Inside the very tip are cells holding tiny heavy grains of starch. The grains sink to the bottom of each cell, like sand in a bottle. So the root can tell which way is down. The shoot grows the other way, up towards the light. In beans, the shoot comes up bent like a hook. The hook protects the soft tip as it pushes through the soil.
examples: Put soaked chana in a jar against wet paper, some upside down. Every root bends to grow down.
Turn the jar on its side after the roots appear. In a day, the root tips bend down again.
A bean shoot pushes up through the soil bent like a hook, then straightens in the light.
explanations.art: A clear jar lined with wet paper, three chana seeds lying different ways, every root curving down and every shoot curving up, with a small zoom showing tiny grains settled at the bottom of root-tip cells.
explanations.context: When a seed sprouts, which part comes out first, and how does it know which way to grow? This card explains.

explanations.concept: Rice: the seed that can start under water
explanations.definition: Rice is unusual. Its seeds can start to sprout even under water, with very little oxygen.
explanations.description: Most seeds drown under water. Rice comes from wet, flooded places, and its seeds have a trick. Under water, a rice seed sends up its first shoot quickly, before its root. The shoot grows up like a snorkel until its tip reaches the air. Then air can travel down it, and the root can start. This helps rice grow in flooded fields. Scientists are still studying exactly how rice does this, so they can help farmers sow rice straight into wet fields.
examples: Moong seeds under water mostly fail. Paddy, rice still in its husk, often sends up a shoot under water. Kitchen rice cannot do this, because milling has removed its baby plant.
In many paddy fields in India, rice grows with its feet in water.
explanations.art: A rice grain at the bottom of a glass of water, a thin pale shoot rising like a snorkel to the surface, beside a moong seed lying still.
explanations.context: Seeds need air to sprout. This card is about one famous exception, rice, and the snorkel trick it uses.

explanations.concept: How long can a seed wait?
explanations.description: A dry, cool seed can stay alive for a long time, but nobody knows the longest. In 1879, a scientist in the United States, William James Beal, buried bottles of seeds in sand. Every few years, someone digs one up and plants the seeds. In 2021, more than 140 years later, some seeds still sprouted. Sacred lotus seeds about 1,300 years old have sprouted in China. In 2005, Elaine Solowey grew a date palm in Israel from a seed about 2,000 years old. It came from the ruins of an ancient fort called Masada. She worked with a doctor, Sarah Sallon, and the tree was named Methuselah. Most seeds do not last nearly this long. Scientists are still finding out what lets some seeds wait for centuries.
examples: Moong from the kitchen usually sprouts well for a year or two, then fewer seeds sprout each year.
Seeds last much longer when they are kept dry and cold. That is why seed banks keep them in freezers.

perspectives.explanation: Old seeds slowly get damaged inside, a little more each year. Dry and cold slow this down. Every kind of seed has its own limit.
A few seeds may be far better at repairing themselves than we know. The real limit could be thousands of years. Nobody has had time to test it.

explanations.art: A young date palm in a pot, beside a glass bottle of old seeds dug out of sand and a lotus flower, with a timeline showing 140 years, 1,300 years and 2,000 years.
explanations.context: A dry seed is asleep. This card asks how long it can sleep and still wake up.

explanations.description: A dry seed does not grow, move or seem to eat. It breathes so slowly that it is very hard to measure. Yet add water, and it wakes up. So is a dry seed alive the whole time, or does it come back to life? Scientists and thinkers answer this in different ways. The question matters, because it tests what we mean by 'alive'.
examples: A moong seed in a jar for a year, and the same seed sprouting two days after soaking.
Tardigrades, tiny water animals about half a millimetre long, can dry out completely and wake up again years later when they get wet.

perspectives.explanation: A dry seed is alive, but dormant. Its cells are still whole and still working, very, very slowly. It is like a person in a very deep sleep.

perspectives.who: Some scientists who study drying out
perspectives.explanation: In a very dry seed, life almost stops. They call this 'hidden life'. The seed is not doing much, but it keeps everything it needs to start again.
The seed shows that 'alive' and 'not alive' may not be two neat boxes. There may be states in between, and our words do not fit them well.

explanations.art: A dry moong seed drawn half as a pebble and half as a sleeping baby plant, with a question mark between them.
explanations.context: Is a seed in a jar alive or not? This card is about a question that scientists and thinkers still answer in different ways.

explanations.concept: Deep down: a seed is stored sunlight
explanations.definition: The food in a seed was made by its parent plant from air, water and sunlight. When the seed sprouts and breathes, it uses that stored sunlight energy and sends the carbon back into the air.
explanations.description: The parent plant's leaves took in carbon dioxide from the air and water from the soil. Using the energy of sunlight, they built sugar and starch. The plant packed some of this food into each seed. When the seed sprouts, it breathes: its cells join the stored food with oxygen. That releases the energy that sunlight first put into the food, and the carbon goes back into the air as carbon dioxide. So a sprout in the dark uses up its food as it grows. Dried out, it weighs less than the seed it came from. It must reach the light, and start making new food, before its store runs out.
examples: Sprout seeds in the dark for a week, then dry them in the sun. They weigh less than the same number of dry seeds that were never sprouted.
The energy in the chana you eat also came from sunlight, stored by the chana plant.
explanations.art: A chain of pictures: the Sun shining on a chana plant's leaves, the plant packing tiny glowing parcels into its seeds, and a sprouting seed releasing the glow and little bubbles back into the air.
explanations.context: This card zooms in on the seed's food store, down to its atoms. It follows the energy all the way back to the Sun.

explanations.concept: How a seed knows when to wake
explanations.description: Some seeds wake as soon as they are wet. Others wait for a sign that the time is right. Some wait for a long cold winter. Some wait until a fire has passed. In 2004, Gavin Flematti and his team in Australia found the chemical in smoke that wakes many such seeds. Some seeds have a coat so hard that it must be scratched, or pass through a bird's belly, before water can get in. Scientists understand parts of how seeds sense these signs. How a seed decides, using many signs at once, is still being worked out.
examples: Apple seeds, and the seeds of many mountain wildflowers, sprout only after weeks of cold.
Some plants of Australia and South Africa sprout in great numbers after a bush fire.
Gardeners rub very hard seeds with sandpaper, or nick them, so that water can get in.

perspectives.explanation: A seed has sensors for water, warmth, light and some chemicals. Its hormones add up these signals, a bit like a set of switches.
This adding up of signals is a simple kind of decision-making without a brain. Others say 'decision' is the wrong word for chemistry. They still argue about it.

explanations.art: Three seeds waiting for different signals: one under snow, one in ash after a fire with a wisp of smoke, one with a hard coat being scratched by sand.
explanations.context: Water, warmth and air wake most seeds. This card is about seeds that wait for a special sign first.

explanations.concept: Seeds in space and on the Moon
explanations.definition: Seeds have travelled into space and come back able to sprout. Seeds have even sprouted on the Moon, inside a sealed box.
explanations.description: In 1971, an astronaut called Stuart Roosa carried about 500 tree seeds around the Moon on the Apollo 14 mission. Back on Earth, many were sprouted and planted. They grew into normal trees, called Moon trees. In January 2019, China's Chang'e 4 lander carried cotton seeds to the far side of the Moon in a sealed box with water, air and soil. A cotton seed sprouted there, the first seed to sprout on the Moon. When the long, freezing lunar night came, it died. It had water and air, but not enough warmth. Space farmers will need all three.
examples: Moon trees from the Apollo 14 seeds still grow in parts of the United States.
The cotton seedling on the Moon died when the temperature fell far below freezing.
explanations.art: A small sealed canister on the grey surface of the Moon, a tiny cotton sprout inside, with the Earth far away in the black sky.
explanations.context: Could seeds sprout away from Earth? This card is about seeds that went to the Moon.

agreed.text: A seed holds a living baby plant, with a coat and a store of food.
agreed.evidence: Split any soaked bean and you can see the baby plant with a hand lens. Scientists have looked at seeds under microscopes for more than 300 years.

agreed.text: Most seeds need water, warmth and air to sprout, and do not need light or soil to start.
agreed.evidence: Fair tests like the five-cup test give the same results in classrooms and laboratories all over the world.

agreed.text: A sprouting seed breathes. It uses oxygen and gives out carbon dioxide and heat.
agreed.evidence: A flask of sprouting seeds warms up, while boiled seeds do not. Scientists can measure the oxygen used and the carbon dioxide given out.

agreed.text: The root comes out first and grows down, and the shoot grows up.
agreed.evidence: Seeds placed any way up in a jar send their roots down. Turn the jar, and the root tips turn down again. In space, where the pull is tiny, roots wander in many directions.

agreed.text: Dry, cool seeds can stay alive for years, and some for centuries.
agreed.evidence: Seeds from Beal's bottles sprouted after more than 140 years. A date palm seed about 2,000 years old was sprouted in 2005, and its age was checked by carbon dating.

challenging.who: Many children and grown-ups. It is a very common guess.
challenging.for: Plants need light to grow well. And seeds in a garden usually sprout where the sun shines.
challenging.against: Moong sprouts in a closed dark tiffin. Seeds in the ground sprout in the dark. A seed carries its own food, so it needs light only once its leaves come up. A few small seeds, like some lettuce, are exceptions.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea: that seeds need sunlight before they can sprout.

challenging.for: We plant seeds in soil, and that is where they grow in nature.
challenging.against: Seeds sprout on wet cloth, cotton or paper. Soil holds water and air and keeps the seed dark and safe. It also feeds the plant later. But the seed does not need it to start.
challenging.context: This card looks at another common idea: that a seed must be in soil to sprout.

challenging.claim: The more water a seed gets, the better it sprouts.
challenging.for: Water is the first thing a seed needs, and dry seeds never sprout.
challenging.against: A seed under water cannot get enough air to breathe. In the five-cup test, the seeds under water do badly, and some go sour. Damp is just right. Rice is the famous exception.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that more water is always better for seeds.

challenging.claim: A dry seed is dead until water brings it to life.
challenging.who: A common way of thinking, because dry seeds do nothing we can see
challenging.for: A dry seed does not grow or move, and it seems to use no food.
challenging.against: A dry seed is still breathing, very slowly. Boiled seeds never sprout, however much water they get. So something in the dry seed was alive all along.
challenging.context: This card asks whether a seed in a jar is dead, or alive and waiting.

challenging.claim: A big seed grows into a big plant.
challenging.for: Big seeds carry more food, so their seedlings often start bigger.
challenging.against: A banyan or peepal seed is smaller than a grain of rai, yet it grows into a giant tree. A big rajma grows into a small plant. A seed is only the start. The plant builds most of its body from air and water, using the energy of sunlight, with a little from the soil.
challenging.context: This card asks if the size of a seed tells you the size of the plant.

challenging.claim: Seeds sprout better if you sow them at the right phase of the Moon.
challenging.who: Some farmers and gardeners around the world, following old planting calendars
challenging.for: The custom is very old. Some people believe the Moon pulls water in the soil, like it pulls the sea.
challenging.against: The Moon's pull on a little patch of soil is far too tiny to move its water. Careful tests have not found a clear effect. Many farmers still follow such calendars, and they may help in other ways, like keeping planting on time.
challenging.context: This card is about an old belief that the Moon's phase changes how seeds sprout.

big_questions.q: A dry seed sits in a jar for a year, doing nothing. Is it alive the whole time? How could you prove it?
big_questions.hint: What happens to a boiled seed when you soak it? What happens to an unboiled one?

big_questions.q: Why does a seed carry its own food, when a grown plant makes food from sunlight?
big_questions.hint: Where is a seed when it first wakes up? Can it see the Sun from there?

big_questions.q: How does a root know which way is down, even in the dark?
big_questions.hint: Think about sand in a bottle. Which way does it settle when you turn the bottle?

big_questions.q: A sprouting seed breathes, like you. What else do you and a seed have in common?
big_questions.hint: Think about food, water, warmth and growing.

big_questions.q: When does a plant's life begin? When the seed sprouts, when the seed was made, or before that?
big_questions.hint: Who made the baby plant inside the seed, and who packed its food store?

big_questions.q: Some seeds sprout as soon as they are wet. Others wait for a cold winter or a fire. Why might it help a seed to wait?
big_questions.hint: What would happen to a seedling that sprouted just before a frost, or in a dry month?

big_questions.q: During a terrible war, scientists guarding a seed bank in Leningrad chose to go hungry rather than eat the seeds. Why would anyone do that?
big_questions.hint: Who were the seeds for? How many people could they feed one day?

big_questions.q: Every chana in your chole was once a living baby plant with its own food store. Does knowing that change how you see your food?
big_questions.hint: Many families say thank you before eating. What might they be thanking?

big_questions.q: A seed about 2,000 years old grew into a date palm. What would that tree tell us, if it could speak?
big_questions.hint: Who was alive when that seed fell? What has changed since?

big_questions.q: If we lived on the Moon or Mars, what would we have to bring for our seeds?
big_questions.hint: Remember the three things every seed needs. Which ones does the Moon not have?

story.title: The Warm Bundle
story.note: Noor, her family and the sprouts cart are made up. The science is real: soaked seeds need air, a heap of sprouting seeds gets warm because it is breathing, and seeds kept under water too long go sour.
text: Every morning at six, Noor's mother pushed a blue handcart to the corner outside Byculla station in Mumbai. On the cart was a big steel bowl of sprouts. There were green moong with white tails, chopped onion, tomato, lemon and a pinch of red chilli. Office workers stopped on their way to the train. 'One plate, Ammi,' they said, and Ammi spooned sprouts into a leaf bowl. Two hundred plates on a good day. On a bad day, fewer.

Noor was nine, and she knew how the sprouts were made, or she thought she did. At night, Ammi poured moong into the big dabba and covered it with water. In the morning she drained it. She tipped the fat, wet seeds into an old white cloth and tied it loosely, like a bundle for a journey. Then she hung it from a nail on the window bars. By the next morning, every seed had a tail.
'Why the nail?' Noor once asked. 'Why not leave them in the dabba?'
'Because they are getting ready to travel,' said Ammi, which was not really an answer. Ammi's answers were often like that.

Then came the week of Khala's wedding in Nashik. Ammi had to go for two days. 'Faiz will run the cart on Sunday,' she said. Faiz was thirteen and thought he was eighteen. 'And Noor will make the sprouts. Soak them tonight. Hang them tomorrow. You have seen me do it a thousand times.'
Noor nodded. A thousand times was a lot.

That night she soaked the moong in the dabba, just as Ammi did. But in the morning, before she could drain it, she heard a scratching under the floorboards. Last month, a rat had chewed through Ammi's bundle on the nail. Half the sprouts had been ruined. Ammi had cried a little, when she thought nobody was looking.
Not this time, Noor decided. She left the moong in its water. She pressed the steel lid down hard. Then she put the heavy grinding stone on top. No rat could lift that. Pleased, she went to school.

When she came home, the room smelled strange. She lifted the stone and the lid. The water had gone cloudy, and a grey froth floated on top. The smell was sour, like milk left out in the heat. The seeds were fat and soft, but not one of them had a tail.
'You killed them,' said Faiz, holding his nose.
'I did not,' said Noor. But her stomach went cold. There was no money to buy more moong. The cart would sell nothing on Sunday, and Ammi would come home to an empty tin.

She sat down on the floor beside the dabba. She tried to remember everything Ammi did, every single step. Soak. Drain. Tie loosely. Hang. And one more thing, a thing she had nearly forgotten. Once, last winter, Ammi had let her hold the bundle before dawn. It had been warm. Not warm from the stove, which was cold. Warm from inside, like a sleeping kitten.
'Why is it warm?' she had asked.
'Because they are breathing,' Ammi had said. 'Everything that wakes up has to breathe.'

Noor looked at the dabba with its lid and its stone and its water. Nothing could get in, not a rat, and not a breath of air either. She thought of the time she had dipped her face in a bucket of water. She could only hold her breath for a few seconds.
'They were drowning,' she said.

She drained the cloudy water at once. She rinsed the seeds under the tap, once, twice, five times, until the sour smell had almost gone. She picked out the ones that were mushy and broken. There were a lot of them. Then she spread the rest on the white cloth and tied it loosely, the way Ammi did, with room for air between the seeds. She hung it from the nail on the window bars, where the sea breeze came in.
'What about the rat?' said Faiz.

Noor fetched Ammi's steel strainer. She hung it upside down on the string above the bundle, like an umbrella. A rat that climbed down the string would slide right off. Faiz looked at it for a long time. Then he said, 'Not bad.'

Noor could not sleep. Twice in the night she got up and touched the bundle. It was cool and damp. At four in the morning she touched it again. And this time, in the very middle, it was warm. Not much. Just a little, like a hand that has been holding another hand.

When the first light came, she untied the cloth. Most of the seeds had split their green coats. Out of each one curled a tiny white tail, thin as a comma in her school book. Not every seed. About two of every three. But that was enough.

On Sunday, Faiz pushed the blue cart to the corner outside the station. Noor chopped the onions and squeezed the lemons. They sold one hundred and thirty plates. It was not two hundred. Faiz said it was a record for a cart run by children, and nobody could prove that it wasn't.
That night, Ammi called from Nashik. Music and laughter roared behind her. 'How were the sprouts?' she shouted.
'They were breathing,' said Noor.
There was a little silence on the line. Then Ammi laughed, the way she laughed when Noor said something she had not expected. 'Of course they were,' she said. 'Did you hang them on the nail?'
'With an umbrella,' said Noor. And she went to the window and laid her hand on the new bundle, soaked and tied and hanging in the dark, already beginning to wake.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the seeds did not fail because they were soaked wrongly. They failed because they could not breathe. A waking seed needs air as well as water, and seeds left sealed under water run out of oxygen and go sour. The warmth Noor remembered was the clue: a heap of sprouting seeds gets warm because millions of cells are breathing, using oxygen to burn their stored food. Water, warmth and air together are what wake a seed. The story also quietly shows how much a child can learn just by watching a parent's ordinary work closely.
ask: Noor shut the moong under a heavy lid to keep the rat out. Why did that stop them sprouting?
The bundle on the nail felt warm in the night. Where did the warmth come from?
Why do you think Ammi always tied the cloth loosely, not tightly?
Noor remembered something Ammi did without explaining it. What have you learnt just by watching someone at home?
Faiz said 'Not bad' about the strainer umbrella. How did Noor solve two problems at once?
