A loosely tied white cloth bundle hanging from a nail on window bars, the sea in the distance.
A steel dabba with a grinding stone on its lid, and cloudy water with grey froth inside.
Noor at four in the morning, in the dark, with her hand on the bundle, a steel strainer hanging above it like an umbrella.
A cloth opened at sunrise, full of green moong with tiny white tails like commas.

games.title: Wake Up, Seed!
games.players: 2 to 4 players, or one child playing against the app
games.context: This is a card game about what a seed needs to sprout. Each player is a sleeping seed. To sprout, you must collect three cards: water, warmth and air.

printables.title: 36 condition cards to cut out
items: WATER: rain soaks into the soil
WATER: a child sprinkles the pot
WATER: dew on a cool morning
WARMTH: the soil warms up in spring
WARMTH: a pot by a warm wall
AIR: a breeze through the window
AIR: seeds spread out, not squashed
SUNLIGHT: bright sun on the soil (keep this card until you sprout, then it makes your leaves grow)
FERTILE SOIL: rich black earth (useful later, not now)
DROWNED: you are under water. Give back one AIR card.
DROWNED: the dabba lid is shut tight. Give back one AIR card.
FROST: a cold night in Shimla. Give back one WARMTH card.
FRIDGE: someone put you in the fridge. Give back one WARMTH card.
DROUGHT: the rain is late. Give back one WATER card.
DRIED OUT: the cloth dried in the sun. Give back one WATER card.
HUNGRY BIRD: a sparrow pecks at you. Miss a turn.
ANT: an ant carries you away. Pass one card to the left.
BOILED: you were cooked for dinner. A boiled seed never sprouts. Start again with no cards.
TEST IT: put one moong seed in water and one on a damp cloth. Which one would you rather be?
TEST IT: hold a soaked bean up to the light. Can you find the little scar where it was joined to its pod?
TEST IT: say which comes out of a seed first: the root or the shoot.
TEST IT: name three seeds you ate this week.
TEST IT: curl up small like a dry seed. Now drink, swell and push out your root.

printables.title: A seed mat for each player
items: A big drawing of a sleeping seed with three empty boxes labelled WATER, WARMTH and AIR

rules: Cut out the 36 cards. Shuffle them and put them face down in a pile.
Each player takes a seed mat. You are a sleeping seed.
On your turn, take the top card and read it out loud.
If it is WATER, WARMTH or AIR, put it in the right box on your mat, if the box is empty. If the box is full, put the card at the bottom of the pile.
SUNLIGHT and FERTILE SOIL cards do not wake a seed. Keep them beside your mat. They count only after you sprout.
Trouble cards make you give back a card or miss a turn. Do what they say.
TEST IT cards: everyone does the test together. The first person to explain it wins a sprout token.
When your three boxes are full, say 'I'm awake!' and explain why each one matters. You win a sprout token, and each SUNLIGHT card you kept wins one more. Clear your mat and start again as a new seed.
When the pile runs out, the player with the most sprout tokens wins.

setup.art: Four paper seed mats on a floor, each with a drawing of a seed and three empty boxes marked with a water drop, a small sun for warmth and an air swirl.
setup.caption: 1. Give each player a seed mat. Put the cards face down.

setup.art: A child placing a card with a water drop picture into the water box on their seed mat.
setup.caption: 2. Take a card. Put WATER, WARMTH or AIR in its box.

setup.art: A child's seed mat with all three boxes full and a green paper leaf token beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Fill all three boxes, say why, and win a sprout token.

flow.do: 1. Give each player a seed mat. 2. Shuffle the 36 cards and put them face down. 3. Put the sprout tokens in a bowl.
flow.say: Each of us is a sleeping seed. To wake up and sprout, a seed needs three things. They are water, warmth and air. Let's see who can wake up first.
flow.kid: You are a sleeping seed. To sprout, you need three cards: WATER, WARMTH and AIR. Put your mat in front of you. Mix the cards.
flow.context: This is the first step of Wake Up, Seed!. It is a card game where each player is a seed collecting what it needs to sprout. Here you set up the game.

flow.do: Before you start, find a SUNLIGHT card and hold it up. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Here is a SUNLIGHT card. Does a seed need sunlight to wake up? What do you think?
flow.kid: Look at the SUNLIGHT card. Does a seed need sunlight to wake up? Tap your answer.

ask.q: Why do you think the game keeps sunlight aside until after the seed sprouts?
good: A seed has its own food, so it doesn't need light at first.
Seeds sprout in the dark, under the soil.
Light is for the leaves, later.

check.q: Does a moong seed need sunlight to sprout?
options: Yes, it cannot sprout without sunlight
No, it can sprout in the dark
check.why: A seed carries its own food store, so it can sprout in the dark, like moong in a closed tiffin. It needs light later, when its green leaves must make food. Picking 'yes' is the most common guess, because grown plants do need light. A few small seeds, like some lettuce, really do need light to wake. Moong does not.

flow.do: 1. Take turns to draw a card and read it out. 2. Place it, or do what it says. 3. When a player fills all three boxes, they say 'I'm awake!' and explain each one.
flow.say: When you wake up, tell us why you needed each card. Why water? Why warmth? Why air?
flow.kid: Take turns. Read your card. Water, warmth or air? Put it in its box. Trouble card? Do what it says. Three full boxes? Say 'I'm awake!' and say why you needed each one.
flow.parent: Good reasons: water softens the coat and wakes the cells. Warmth makes the changes inside the seed go faster. Air gives the seed oxygen to breathe and get energy from its food. The BOILED card is a good talking point: a boiled seed has water, warmth and air, but it never sprouts. Ask why. The baby plant inside has been killed by the heat.

flow.do: When a TEST IT card comes up, stop and do it together. Everyone guesses first.
flow.say: Everyone guess first. Then let's try it and see.
flow.kid: A TEST IT card! Guess first. Then try it. Were you right?

ask.q: The DROWNED card takes away AIR, even though the seed has lots of water. Why?
good: Under water a seed can't get enough air to breathe.
Too much water drowns a seed.

flow.think: Rice seeds can start to grow under water. How do you think they get air?

flow.do: Count the sprout tokens to find the winner. Then look at the SUNLIGHT and FERTILE SOIL cards together.
flow.say: These cards were useful, but not for waking up. When does a plant need sunlight and good soil?
flow.kid: Count your tokens. Who won? Now look at the SUNLIGHT and SOIL cards. When does a plant need them?
flow.think: A seed has its own food store. When does that food run out?

games.title: Seed or Not a Seed?
games.players: 2 to 6 players, or one child with the app
games.context: This is a sorting game with real things from the kitchen. Players decide which of them are seeds, which hold a baby plant and could sprout, and which are not seeds at all.

printables.title: 20 kitchen cards (or use the real things)
Three sorting mats
items: SEED: but could not sprout any more

printables.title: A table to write each guess and what happened when you tested it
items: Tested on a wet cloth: did it sprout?

rules: Lay out the three mats. Shuffle the cards, or put the real things in small bowls.
Take turns to pick one and say which mat it goes on, and why.
Other players can say 'I disagree!' and give a reason. Then check the answer in the app.
A right answer with a good reason wins a point. Changing your mind for a good reason also wins a point.
Afterwards, put a few of each small seed on a wet cloth for two days and find out who was right.

setup.art: Three paper mats on a kitchen floor, one with a sprouting seed picture, one with a seed and a cross, one with a crossed-out seed, and small steel bowls of moong, dal, peanuts, rice and an onion.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the three mats and the kitchen things.

setup.art: A child holding up a peanut and pointing at the sprouting seed mat while another child raises a hand to disagree.
setup.caption: 2. Pick one, choose a mat and say why.

setup.art: A wet cloth on a plate with small groups of moong, split dal and peanuts, labelled with paper slips.
setup.caption: 3. Test your guesses on a wet cloth for two days.

flow.do: 1. Lay out the three mats. 2. Put out the cards, or small amounts of the real things.
flow.say: A seed is a baby plant with a coat and a store of food. Some things in our kitchen are seeds, and some are not. And some seeds can't sprout any more. Let's sort them.
flow.kid: Put out the three mats. Look at the kitchen things. Which are seeds? Which could still sprout?
flow.context: This is the first step of Seed or Not a Seed?. It is a sorting game with kitchen things. Here you set out the mats.

flow.do: Start with whole moong and split moong dal. Play them together as a practice round.
flow.say: Whole moong and split moong dal. They are the same plant. Can both of them sprout?
flow.kid: Look at whole moong and split moong dal. Can both of them sprout? Tap your answer.

check.q: Whole moong and split moong dal. Which one can sprout?
check.why: Whole moong still has its coat and its baby plant. Split dal has had its coat taken off and the seed split in half. The tiny baby plant usually breaks off and is lost. So the dal is only the food store, with no baby plant to grow. Picking 'both' usually means thinking of the seed as just food. A seed needs a living baby plant to sprout.

flow.do: 1. Take turns. Each player picks a thing and puts it on a mat. 2. They say why. 3. Others may disagree. 4. Check with the answers below.
flow.say: Tell me why you chose that mat. Is there a baby plant inside? Is it still alive?
flow.kid: Take turns. Pick one. Put it on a mat. Say why. Does it still have a living baby plant inside?
flow.parent: Answers. SEED, could sprout: whole moong, rajma, raw peanut, paddy, rai, methi and a maize kernel. Coconut is a seed too. A whole coconut in its husk can sprout, but it takes months. Jeera and black pepper are tiny dry fruits, each holding a seed. They sprout slowly or not at all, because spices are dried and stored for a long time. SEED, could not sprout: split moong dal (no baby plant), roasted peanut (cooked), popped popcorn (burst), and polished white rice (milling removed the baby plant). Cashew is a seed, but the ones we buy have been heated to take off their shell. NOT A SEED: a potato is a swollen underground stem, and an onion and a garlic clove are bulbs, short stems with fat leaves. All three can still grow into new plants, but not from a seed. Sabudana is made from the starch of a root, the tapioca. Sugar is made from sugarcane juice.

flow.do: Choose one thing each that you are unsure about. Put a few of each on a wet cloth. Look again in two days.
flow.say: Let's test the ones we argued about. Science settles arguments by testing.
flow.kid: Pick the ones you argued about. Put a few on a wet cloth. Check in two days. Who was right?
flow.think: A potato can grow into a new plant, but it is not a seed. How else can plants make new plants?

items.p: What are the three main parts of a seed?
opts: Seed coat, baby plant and food store
items.why: Every seed has a coat outside, a tiny baby plant inside, and a store of food for it. Picking 'root, stem and flower' mixes up a seed with a grown plant. Those parts grow later.
items.art: A split bean with three labels.

items.p: The tough outer skin of a seed is called the seed ____.
items.why: The seed coat protects the baby plant and keeps it dry until it is time to grow.

items.p: You split a soaked bean in two. What is the tiny thing at one edge, with a little root and two small leaves?
items.why: That is the baby plant, which scientists call the embryo. It was already inside the seed before you soaked it. Picking 'food store' is close, but the food store is the two big halves around it.

items.p: What do most seeds need to sprout?
items.why: Water wakes the seed, warmth makes the changes inside it go faster, and air lets it breathe. Picking 'sunlight and soil' is the most common mistake. A seed has its own food, so it does not need them to start.

items.p: In the five-cup test, you put 10 moong seeds in each of 5 cups: dry, damp, damp in the fridge, under water with oil on top, and damp in the light. In which cup did the most seeds sprout?
items.why: The damp, warm cup had water, warmth and air together. Picking 'under water' usually means thinking more water is always better. Those seeds could not get enough air.
items.context: In the five-cup test, you put 10 moong seeds in each of 5 cups: dry, damp, damp in the fridge, under water with oil on top, and damp in the light.

items.p: Moong seeds can sprout in a dark cupboard.
items.why: True. A seed carries its own food, so it does not need light to sprout. In the five-cup test, the cup in the dark did as well as the cup in the light.

items.p: Seeds need soil before they can sprout.
items.why: False. Seeds sprout on wet cotton, cloth or paper. Soil helps later, by holding water and the plant's roots.

items.p: Which part comes out of a sprouting seed first?
items.why: The root comes out first, so the seedling can hold on and drink. Picking 'leaves' is common, because leaves are what we see first above the soil.

items.p: A seed waking up and starting to grow is called ____.
items.why: Germination is the scientists' word for a seed sprouting.

items.p: Sort these. Could they still sprout, or not?
items.why: A seed can sprout only if its baby plant is whole and alive. Splitting the dal loses the baby plant. Roasting and popping kill it.

items.p: A seed is put in a cup full of water, right up to the top. What usually happens?
opts: It sprouts best, because it has the most water
It does badly, because it cannot get enough air
It turns into a plant overnight
items.why: Seeds need air to breathe. Under water there is very little air, so most seeds do badly or rot. Picking 'sprouts best' means thinking more water is always better. Rice is an exception.

items.p: Why does a bean seed have two fat halves full of food?
opts: To feed the baby plant until its leaves can make food
To make the seed heavy so it doesn't blow away
items.why: The food store feeds the baby plant while it is still underground, with no light. Animals do eat seeds, but that is not why the seed has food. The food is for the baby plant.

items.p: Your friend says, 'Dry seeds in a jar are dead.' What would you tell them? Give one piece of evidence.
items.a: Dry seeds are alive, but asleep. My evidence: when we soaked moong from a jar, most of it sprouted in two days. Boiled seeds never sprout, so the jar seeds must have been alive.
items.why: A good answer says the seeds are alive but resting, and gives evidence, such as the seeds sprouting once they got water.

items.p: Put these in order, from first to last, as a bean sprouts.
items: The seed drinks water and swells
The root comes out and grows down
The shoot comes up, bent like a hook
The first leaves open in the light
items.why: First the seed drinks and swells, which splits the coat. The root comes first, then the shoot. Leaves open last, once the shoot reaches the light.

items.p: Draw a seed opened in half. Label the seed coat, the baby plant and the food store.
items.a: A bean shape split open, with the coat peeling off, two large halves labelled 'food store' and a tiny plant at one edge labelled 'baby plant'.
items.why: Every seed has these three parts.
items.art: An empty outline of a bean.

items.p: Why do we put 10 seeds in each cup, not just 1?
opts: Because one seed might be a dud, and 10 give a fairer answer
items.why: Some seeds don't sprout even when everything is right. If we used only one, a single dud seed could fool us. With 10, one dud matters much less.

items.p: A heap of sprouting moong in a cloth gets warm. Why?
opts: The seeds are breathing, and breathing makes a little heat
The cloth is made of wool
items.why: Sprouting seeds use oxygen to get energy from their food, and some energy comes out as heat. Picking 'rotting' is a good guess, because rotting things do warm up. But healthy sprouts warm up too, and boiled seeds do not.

items.p: In the warm flask test, why did we use boiled seeds in the second flask?
opts: So the only difference between the flasks was whether the seeds were alive
items.why: A fair test changes only one thing. Both flasks had the same wet seeds, but only one lot was alive. So any difference in warmth must come from being alive. Picking 'sprout faster' is wrong. Boiled seeds never sprout.

items.p: The gas in the air that sprouting seeds need to breathe is called ____.
items.why: Seeds, like us, use oxygen from the air to get energy from food.

items.p: In the swelling test, 50 grams of dry chana weighed about 100 grams after soaking. How many times heavier was it?
items.why: 100 is 2 lots of 50. So the soaked chana was 2 times as heavy. The extra 50 grams is water inside the seeds.

items.p: A jar packed with dry chana and water can push its lid off overnight.
items.why: True. Swelling seeds push very hard as they soak up water. That is why we use a plastic cup, never glass.

items.p: Your seeds on damp cotton in the fridge hardly sprouted. Then you moved them to the kitchen shelf. What will most likely happen?
opts: They will start to sprout, because cold only made them wait
Nothing, because the cold killed them
items.why: Cold slows the changes inside a seed, but usually does not kill it. Once it is warm, it wakes up. Picking 'the cold killed them' is a common guess. Try it and see.

items.p: Match each cup in the five-cup test to what it was missing.
pairs: nothing missing, it had extra light
items.why: Each cup was different from the damp, warm cup in just one way. That way we can tell what each thing does.

items.p: A root always grows down, even if the seed is upside down. How does the root know which way is down?
opts: Its tip feels gravity, using tiny heavy grains that settle at the bottom of its cells
It follows the smell of soil
It doesn't know, it just grows any way
items.why: Cells in the root tip hold tiny heavy grains of starch. They sink to the bottom, like sand in a bottle, so the root can tell which way is down. Picking 'see' is not right. A root has no eyes, and it turns down even in a dark jar.

items.p: Why do sprouts taste a little sweet?
opts: The seed has turned some of its starch into sugar
items.why: As a seed sprouts, enzymes, helpers made by its cells, cut starch into sugar the baby plant can use. That's why ragi malt is made from sprouted ragi.

items.p: Rice seeds are unusual. What can they do that most seeds can't?
opts: Start to sprout under water, sending a shoot up like a snorkel
items.why: Rice comes from wet places. Under water, its first shoot grows up to the air like a snorkel, so air can reach the rest of the seedling. Most seeds would drown.

items.p: Noor's mother hung her moong in a loose cloth bundle, not in a closed tin. Why is that better for sprouting? Use the word air in your answer.
items.a: In a loose cloth, air can reach every seed, so the seeds can breathe. In a closed tin full of water, they get very little air and go sour.
items.why: A good answer says that seeds need air to breathe, and a loose cloth lets air in.
items.context: In the story The Warm Bundle, Noor's mother makes sprouts for her cart. She soaks moong, then ties it loosely in a cloth and hangs it from a nail.

items.p: A big rajma bean and a tiny banyan seed. Which grows into the bigger plant?
opts: The banyan seed, which grows into a giant tree
The rajma, because its seed is bigger
items.why: The size of a seed does not tell you the size of the plant. A tiny banyan seed can become a huge tree. The plant builds itself mostly from air and water, using sunlight, over many years.

items.p: Draw the seed window jar after 5 days. Show 3 seeds that started in different ways, with their roots and shoots.
items.a: Three seeds, each with a root curving down and a shoot curving up, whichever way the seed was placed.
items.why: Roots grow towards gravity and shoots grow away from it.

items.p: Plan a fair test to find out if methi seeds need warmth to sprout. What will you change? What will you keep the same?
items.a: I will change only the warmth: one cup in the fridge and one on the kitchen shelf. I will keep the same: the number of methi seeds, the same cotton, the same amount of water, and both cups dark.
items.why: A good fair test changes just one thing and keeps everything else the same. Keeping both cups dark matters, because the fridge is dark.

items.p: Old seeds from Beal's bottles, buried in 1879, still sprouted in 2021.
items.why: True. More than 140 years later, some of the seeds sprouted. Dry seeds in the ground can stay alive for a very long time.

items.p: Deep down, where did the energy in a seed's food store come from?
opts: From sunlight, captured by the parent plant's leaves
From the water the seed drinks
items.why: The parent plant used the energy of sunlight to make starch from air and water, and packed it into the seed. Picking 'soil' is a very old idea. Soil gives a plant water and small amounts of minerals, but not its food energy.

items.p: You sprout 50 moong seeds in the dark for a week, then dry them. Do they weigh more or less than 50 dry seeds that were never sprouted?
opts: Less, because they burned some of their stored food by breathing
items.why: In the dark, sprouts cannot make new food. They use up their stored food by breathing, and the carbon goes into the air. So once the water is dried out, they weigh less. Picking 'more' is the usual guess, because sprouts look bigger. Most of that size is water.

items.p: A seed sealed under water goes sour. A seed in a dry jar does nothing. A seed on damp cotton sprouts. Explain all three using what a seed needs.
items.a: Under water, the seed has water but no air, so it cannot breathe, and it goes sour. In a dry jar, it has air but no water, so it stays asleep. On damp cotton, it has water and air, and the room is warm, so it sprouts.
items.why: A good answer names what each seed has and what it is missing.

items.p: Some small lettuce seeds will sprout only if light reaches them. Why might a tiny seed wait for light?
opts: Light tells it it is near the surface, so its small food store won't run out before it reaches the sun
Light gives it food straight away
items.why: A tiny seed has only a little food. If it sprouted deep underground, it might run out before reaching the light. So waiting for light keeps it safe. In 1952, scientists in the United States showed that red light is what wakes these seeds.

items.p: Match each scientist to what they found.
pairs: buried bottles of seeds to see how long they live
grew a date palm from a 2,000-year-old seed
found the message a baby plant sends to its food store
found the chemical in smoke that wakes some seeds
items.why: Each of these scientists helped us understand how seeds wait and wake.

items.p: In 2019, a cotton seed sprouted on the Moon inside China's Chang'e 4 lander.
items.why: True. It sprouted in a sealed box with water, air and soil, then died when the freezing lunar night came. It had water and air, but not enough warmth.

items.p: Is a dry seed in a jar alive? Give one reason to say yes, and one reason someone might say no.
items.a: Yes: it is still breathing very slowly, and it sprouts when we add water, unlike a boiled seed. Someone might say no: it does not grow, move or seem to eat.
items.why: There is no single right answer. Scientists mostly say it is alive but dormant. What counts is a reason on each side.

items.p: A heap of sprouting seeds warms up. A heap of boiled seeds stays cool for a day, then starts to warm and smell. Why does the boiled heap start to warm?
opts: Tiny living things called bacteria start feeding on it, and they breathe too
The boiled seeds come back to life
items.why: Boiled seeds are dead, but bacteria can feed on them. Bacteria breathe, so they make warmth too. That is why we stop the warm flask test after 2 days.

items.p: Why do you think seed banks keep seeds dry and very cold?
items.a: Dry and cold slow everything inside the seed down, so the seed uses its food very slowly and stays asleep. Then it can stay alive for many years, until someone needs it.
items.why: Warmth and water wake a seed. Taking them away keeps it asleep.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out? Rajma, chana, moong, potato.
items.why: Rajma, chana and moong are seeds, each with a baby plant inside. A potato is a swollen underground stem. It can grow new plants, but it is not a seed.

items.p: Rahibai Soma Popere, a farmer in Maharashtra, saves the seeds of many old local kinds of crops. Why does keeping many kinds matter?
opts: If a disease or drought kills one kind, other kinds may survive
It makes the seeds sprout faster
items.why: Different kinds of the same crop cope with different problems. If every farmer grew just one kind, one disease could wipe out the whole harvest. For this work, she was given the Padma Shri in 2020.

items.p: A farmer stores seed paddy in a damp, warm corner of the house. Next season, very few seeds sprout. What went wrong?
items.a: Damp and warmth woke the seeds up too early, or made them use up their food and spoil while stored. Seeds keep best when dry and cool.
items.why: Water and warmth wake seeds. In storage, we want them to stay asleep.

items.p: Invent a seed for a desert where it rains only once every few years. Draw it and label two features that help it wait and then sprout fast.
items.a: Any thoughtful design, for example: a very hard waterproof coat so it can wait for years, a coat that only softens after lots of rain, a big food store so the root can grow fast and deep.
items.why: Real desert seeds do things like these. Many wait in the sand until a big rain, then sprout and flower in a few weeks.
items.art: An empty patch of desert sand.

items.p: In the story The Warm Bundle, Noor remembered the bundle being warm. How did that clue help her save the sprouts?
items.a: Ammi said the warmth came from the seeds breathing. So Noor realised the seeds needed air. In the closed dabba under water, they could not breathe. She drained them and hung them in a loose cloth so air could reach them.
items.why: The warmth showed that sprouting seeds breathe. Breathing needs air.
items.context: In the story The Warm Bundle, Noor tries to make sprouts while her mother is away. She seals the moong under water to protect it from rats, and it goes sour.

items.p: Astronauts on the Moon want to grow beans. List what they must give the seeds to sprout, and what the young plants will need later.
items.a: To sprout: water, warmth and air, inside a sealed box or base. Later: light for the leaves to make food, and minerals, like those in soil or plant food.
items.why: A seed needs water, warmth and air to wake. A seedling needs light once its own food store runs out.

experiments.title: The Five-Cup Test: what wakes a seed?
experiments.context: This is the five-cup test. You put 10 moong seeds in each of 5 cups. Each cup is missing one thing a seed might need, or has one thing extra. After 3 days you count which seeds sprouted.
experiments.question: What does a moong seed need to sprout? Water? Warmth? Air? Light?
experiments.predict: Before you start, look at the five cups. Guess how many of the 10 seeds will sprout in each cup, and say why you think so. Write your guesses down.
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, every cup gets the same kind of seeds, the same number of seeds and the same cotton. Each cup changes only one thing compared with the damp, warm cup. We use 10 seeds in each cup, not 1, because one seed might be a dud.

materials.item: 50 whole moong seeds (not dal), from the same packet
5 small cups, katoris or clear plastic cups, all the same
cotton wool or folded tissue paper
water, a spoon and a little cooking oil
4 steel plates or lids to cover cups 1 to 4, and a clear plastic bag or clear lid for cup 5
stickers or slips of paper and a pen for labels

experiments.safety: A grown-up boils the water for cup 4 and lets it cool completely. Do not eat the seeds used in this test. Throw away any seeds that smell sour.

schedule.what: Set up the five cups. Write your guesses.
Count the seeds with a root in each cup. Keep cups 2, 3 and 5 damp.
Count again. Draw a bar chart. Say what you think, what you saw and why. Move the fridge cup to the shelf and wet the dry cup.

experiments.record: Fill in the table each day. On day 3, draw a bar chart with one bar for each cup. Make each bar as tall as the number of seeds that sprouted.

setup.art: Five identical clear cups in a row, each with a cotton pad and ten green moong seeds, with paper labels: Dry, Damp, Fridge, Under water, Light.
setup.caption: 1. Put cotton and 10 moong seeds in each of 5 cups. Label them.

setup.art: A hand sprinkling water on cotton in three cups, a fourth cup filled to the top with water and a thin layer of oil floating on top, and a fifth cup left dry.
setup.caption: 2. Wet cups 2, 3 and 5. Fill cup 4 with cooled boiled water and a little oil. Leave cup 1 dry.

setup.art: Three cups covered with steel plates on a kitchen shelf, one cup covered with a plate inside an open fridge, and one cup under a clear plastic cover on a bright window sill, out of direct sun.
setup.caption: 3. Cover cups 1, 2 and 4 with plates. Put cup 3, covered, in the fridge. Cover cup 5 with clear plastic and put it in the light.

setup.art: A child counting moong seeds with little white tails in each cup, writing in a table.
setup.caption: 4. On days 2 and 3, count the seeds with a root.

example_chart.title: Made-up example: how many of 10 moong seeds sprouted in 3 days
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

flow.context: This is the first step of the five-cup test. You set up 5 cups of moong seeds to find out what a seed needs to sprout.
flow.do: 1. Put a thin layer of cotton in each of the 5 cups. 2. Count 10 moong seeds onto the cotton in each cup. 3. Label the cups: 1 Dry, 2 Damp, 3 Fridge, 4 Under water, 5 Light.
flow.say: We're going to find out what wakes a seed. Each cup is a little different. Let's count 10 seeds into each one.
flow.kid: Put cotton in 5 cups. Count 10 moong seeds into each cup. Label them: Dry, Damp, Fridge, Under water, Light.

flow.do: 1. Cup 1: no water. 2. Cups 2, 3 and 5: add water a spoon at a time. Stop when the cotton is wet but no water lies on top. 3. Cup 4: a grown-up boils some water and lets it cool. Fill cup 4 to the top with it. Pour a thin layer of oil on top.
flow.say: Boiling pushes out most of the air in water. The oil stops new air getting back in. So cup 4 has lots of water but very little air.
flow.kid: Cup 1 stays dry. Make cups 2, 3 and 5 damp, not swimming. Ask a grown-up for cooled boiled water for cup 4. Fill it up. Add a little oil on top.
flow.parent: Boiling removes much of the air dissolved in water, and oil slows air getting back in. It is not perfect, so a few seeds may still sprout in cup 4. That is fine, and worth talking about. Use whole moong from a packet bought in the last year. Old moong sprouts poorly.

flow.do: 1. Cover cups 1, 2 and 4 with steel plates and put them on a kitchen shelf. 2. Cover cup 3 with a plate and put it in the fridge, not the freezer. 3. Cover cup 5 with a clear plastic bag or lid, and put it in a bright spot out of hot direct sun. 4. Write your guesses in the table, with a reason for each.
flow.say: Cup 2 is our normal cup. Each other cup is different in just one way. Which one is missing water? Which is missing warmth? Which is missing air? Which has extra light? How many will sprout in each, and why do you think so?
flow.kid: Cover cups 1, 2 and 4 with plates. Put cup 3 in the fridge. Put cup 5 in a bright spot, under clear plastic. Guess how many will sprout in each cup. Say why.

ask.q: Why do we compare every cup with cup 2?
good: Cup 2 has everything, so it shows what normal looks like.
Each other cup changes just one thing, so we know what made the difference.

check.q: In the five-cup test, which cup tests whether seeds need air?
check.why: Cup 4 has plenty of water and warmth, but almost no air, because the boiled water and the oil keep air out. So it tests air. Picking cup 1 usually mixes up water and air. Cup 1 has air but no water. Cup 3 tests warmth, and cup 5 tests light.

flow.parent: Every cup is covered, so they all dry out at the same slow rate. Cup 5 has a clear cover, so light gets in. In cold weather, when the room is below about 20 degrees Celsius, as in a North Indian winter, moong sprouts slowly. Then keep cups 1, 2, 4 and 5 in the warmest place you have, such as on top of the fridge or in a kitchen cupboard near the stove, and count on days 3, 4 and 5 instead.

flow.do: 1. The next day, count the seeds with a little white root in each cup. 2. Write the numbers in the table. 3. Add a few drops of water to cups 2, 3 and 5 if the cotton feels dry.
flow.say: Let's count. A seed counts as sprouted when you can see a little white root poking out.
flow.kid: Count the seeds with a white tail in each cup. Write the numbers down. Is any cotton dry? Add a few drops.
flow.parent: By day 2, many seeds in cups 2 and 5 have a root. By day 3, most do. Cup 3 is usually still asleep. Cup 1 seeds look just as they did. Cup 4 seeds are swollen, but most have no root. If fewer than half the seeds in cup 2 sprout by day 3 in warm weather, the moong is probably old. Try again with a fresh packet.

flow.wait: Leave the cups for 1 more day
flow.do: 1. On day 3, count again and write the numbers. 2. Help your child draw a bar chart with one bar for each cup.
flow.say: Let's turn the numbers into a picture. Each cup gets one bar. The taller the bar, the more seeds sprouted.
flow.kid: Count again. Draw one bar for each cup. Make it as tall as the number that sprouted.

chart.title: Made-up example: how many of 10 moong seeds sprouted in 3 days
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

check.q: In the five-cup test, the damp cup in the light and the damp cup in the dark both sprouted about the same. What does that tell you?
options: Moong seeds need light to sprout
Moong seeds do not need light to sprout
check.why: If light mattered, the cup in the light would have sprouted much more. It didn't. So moong seeds sprout just as well in the dark. Picking 'need light' usually comes from knowing that grown plants need light. That is true later, but not for waking up.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened. Then take cup 3 out of the fridge and put it on the shelf. Add water to the dry cup 1 too. Look at both again in 2 days.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think seeds need? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened? Then let's warm the fridge cup and water the dry cup. Will those seeds wake up now?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why. Then take the fridge cup out. Add water to the dry cup. Will they wake up now?
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: moong seeds need water, warmth and air, but not light. What I saw: 9 of 10 sprouted in the damp cups, but none in the dry cup, 1 in the fridge and 2 under water. Why: water wakes the seed, warmth makes it work faster, and it needs air to breathe. The fridge seeds and the dry seeds usually sprout within 2 days of being warmed or wetted. That shows they were alive all along, only waiting.
flow.think: The fridge seeds and the dry seeds woke up once they got what was missing. Were they alive all along?

experiments.title: The Warm Flask: do sprouting seeds breathe?
experiments.context: This is the warm flask test. You put live sprouting moong in one flask and boiled moong in another. A thermometer in each shows whether the live seeds make warmth by breathing.
experiments.question: Do sprouting seeds make warmth? Is that a sign that they are breathing?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. After a day, will the two flasks be the same temperature, or will one be warmer? Which one, and why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, both flasks get the same kind and amount of seeds, soaked for the same time. Both stay in the same place. The only difference is that one lot is alive and the other has been boiled.

materials.item: 2 cups of whole moong, soaked overnight
2 vacuum flasks or 2 insulated casseroles of the same kind and size. Ordinary steel tumblers will not work, because they let the warmth out.

2 thermometers that read room temperature, such as room thermometers or kitchen probe thermometers, or 1 moved between the flasks. A fever thermometer will not work, because most show nothing below 32 degrees.
cotton wool to plug the top of each flask loosely
a pan and a stove, used only by a grown-up

experiments.safety: Only a grown-up boils the seeds. Let them cool completely before they go in a flask. Plug the flasks loosely with cotton, never with a tight lid, so air can get in. Don't eat the seeds afterwards.

schedule.what: Boil and cool one lot of soaked seeds. Fill both flasks. Read both thermometers.
Read both thermometers in the morning and evening.
Read again. Draw two bars for the 24-hour readings. Say what you think, what you saw and why.

experiments.record: Write the temperatures in the table each time. Then draw two bars for the 24-hour reading: one for the live seeds and one for the boiled seeds.

setup.art: Two bowls of soaked moong, one being poured into a steaming pan by a grown-up, the other left as it is.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up boils one bowl of soaked moong, then lets it cool.

setup.art: Two steel flasks side by side, one labelled LIVE and one labelled BOILED, each filled with moong, a thermometer standing in each, and a loose plug of cotton at the top.
setup.caption: 2. Fill one flask with live seeds and one with boiled seeds. Put a thermometer in each.

setup.art: A child reading the red lines on two thermometers, the one in the LIVE flask a little higher.
setup.caption: 3. Read both thermometers, morning and evening, for 2 days.

example_chart.title: Made-up example: temperature inside two flasks of soaked moong (degrees Celsius)
example_chart.note: Made-up numbers to show the pattern. The live sprouts warm up. The boiled seeds stay at about room temperature.

flow.context: This is the first step of the warm flask test. You find out whether sprouting seeds make warmth, by comparing live seeds with boiled ones.
flow.do: 1. Split the soaked moong into two equal bowls. 2. A grown-up boils one bowl for 10 minutes. 3. Let the boiled seeds cool completely, until they feel as cool as the live ones.
flow.say: Boiling kills the baby plants inside the seeds. So these boiled seeds are just the same as the live ones, except they are no longer alive.
flow.kid: Split the soaked moong into two bowls. Ask a grown-up to boil one bowl. Wait until it is cool.

ask.q: Why do we use boiled seeds, and not an empty flask?
good: So the only difference is being alive.
The boiled seeds are wet and the same size, but they can't breathe.

flow.do: 1. Fill one flask nearly to the top with live seeds and label it LIVE. 2. Fill the other the same way with boiled seeds and label it BOILED. 3. Push a thermometer into the middle of each. 4. Plug each top loosely with cotton, or leave the casserole lid slightly open. 5. Read both thermometers and the room temperature. Write them down.
flow.say: The cotton lets air in, but keeps the warmth in the flask. Let's read the thermometers now, at the start.
flow.kid: Fill the LIVE flask and the BOILED flask. Push a thermometer into each. Plug the tops loosely with cotton. Read both numbers. Write them down.
flow.parent: Read the number at the top of the red line. At the start, both flasks should be about the same as the room.

flow.wait: Check morning and evening for 2 days
flow.do: Read both thermometers each morning and evening for 2 days. Write each reading in the table.
flow.say: Are they still the same? Which one is changing?
flow.kid: Read both thermometers, morning and evening. Write the numbers. Which flask is warmer?

chart.title: Made-up example: temperature inside two flasks of soaked moong (degrees Celsius)
chart.note: Made-up numbers to show the pattern. The live sprouts warm up. The boiled seeds stay at about room temperature.

flow.parent: Live sprouting seeds usually warm up by a few degrees in a day. The boiled seeds stay close to the room temperature. If the difference is less than 1 degree, the flask was probably not full enough, because a small heap makes too little warmth. In winter, the live seeds warm up more slowly, so keep reading for the full 2 days. If the boiled seeds start to smell or warm up after a few days, tiny living things called bacteria have started to feed on them. Bacteria breathe too. So stop the test after 2 days.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why.
flow.say: What do you think? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: sprouting seeds breathe, and breathing makes warmth. What I saw: the live seeds warmed up from 27 to 31 degrees, but the boiled seeds stayed at 27. Why: live seeds use oxygen to get energy from their food, and some of that energy comes out as heat.

check.q: In the warm flask test, the flask of live sprouts got warmer than the flask of boiled seeds. Why?
options: The live seeds were breathing, and breathing makes warmth
The boiled seeds were still cooling down
The live flask was in the sun
check.why: Live seeds use oxygen to get energy from their stored food. Some of that energy comes out as heat, so the flask warms. Picking 'still cooling down' is a good scientist's worry, which is why we cooled the boiled seeds first. Picking 'in the sun' would mean the test was not fair. Both flasks were kept in the same place.

experiments.title: The Swelling Push: how much water does a seed drink?
experiments.context: This is the swelling test. You weigh some dry chana, soak it overnight and weigh it again. You also find out how hard swelling seeds can push.
experiments.question: How much water does a seed drink before it sprouts? How hard can a swelling seed push?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. After a night in water, will the chana weigh the same, a little more, or twice as much? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Weigh the chana on the same scale both times. Before you weigh the soaked chana, drain it and pat it dry with a cloth, so you weigh only the water inside the seeds, not the water on the outside.

materials.item: a kitchen scale
50 grams of dry whole chana
a small plastic box or cup with a snap-on lid, such as an empty chutney or takeaway box, not glass
water, a strainer and a cloth

experiments.safety: Use plastic, never glass, for the pushing test. Swelling seeds can crack glass.

schedule.what: Weigh the dry chana and soak it. Fill a small plastic box to the brim with dry chana and water, and snap its lid on.
Weigh the soaked chana. Look at the lid of the full cup. Work out how many times heavier the chana is.

experiments.record: Write both weights. Draw the full cup before and after.

setup.art: 50 grams of dry chana in a steel bowl on a kitchen scale showing 50.
setup.caption: 1. Weigh 50 grams of dry chana.

setup.art: A small clear plastic cup filled to the brim with dry chana and water, its lid pressed on.
setup.caption: 2. Soak the chana. Also fill a small plastic box to the brim with chana and water, and put on its lid.

setup.art: Next morning: the drained chana on the scale showing about 100, and the plastic cup with its lid pushed up by fat swollen chana.
setup.caption: 3. Next day, drain, pat dry and weigh again. Look at the lid.

flow.context: This is the first step of the swelling test. You weigh dry chana before soaking it.
flow.do: 1. Weigh out 50 grams of dry chana. 2. Put it in a bowl and cover it with plenty of water. 3. Write down the weight.
flow.say: Dry seeds have very little water inside. Let's find out how much they drink overnight.
flow.kid: Weigh 50 grams of dry chana. Write it down. Cover it with lots of water.

flow.do: 1. Fill a small plastic box right to the top with dry chana. 2. Pour in water to the brim. 3. Snap the lid on.
flow.say: This box is full to the top. What will happen when the seeds swell? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Fill a small plastic box with dry chana, right to the top. Add water to the top. Put the lid on. What will happen? Why?

flow.do: 1. The next morning, drain the chana in the bowl and pat it dry with a cloth. 2. Weigh it again and write the weight. 3. Look at the box with the lid.
flow.say: How much does it weigh now? Where did the extra weight come from? And look at that lid!
flow.kid: Drain the chana. Pat it dry. Weigh it again. Is it heavier? Now look at the box. What happened to the lid?
flow.parent: The chana usually weighs about twice as much, close to 100 grams. The extra weight is water that went inside the seeds. The lid is usually pushed up or off, and the box may bulge. Swelling seeds push very hard. In cold weather, soak for a full 12 hours.

flow.do: Work out together how many times heavier the chana is. Then ask your child to say what they think, what they saw and why.
flow.say: 50 grams became about 100 grams. How many 50s make 100? So how many times heavier is it?
flow.kid: Dry: 50 grams. Soaked: about 100 grams. How many times heavier? Then say what you think, what you saw and why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: seeds drink a lot of water before they sprout. What I saw: 50 grams of chana became 100 grams, twice as heavy, and the seeds pushed the lid off. Why: water goes inside the seed and it swells.

check.q: In the swelling test, 50 grams of dry chana weighed about 100 grams after soaking. Where did the extra weight come from?
options: Water that went inside the seeds
The seeds grew new food overnight
Air that got into the seeds
check.why: The seeds drank water and swelled. We patted them dry, so the extra weight is the water inside them. Picking 'new food' usually means thinking the seed is already growing. It hasn't made any new food. In fact it starts using its food up. Air weighs far too little to add 50 grams.

activities.title: Open a Seed: find the baby plant and its food store
activities.context: This is a hands-on look inside seeds. You soak some beans and a peanut overnight, peel them, split them open and find the tiny baby plant and its food store.

materials.item: 4 rajma or big white beans, soaked overnight, and 1 dry one to compare
2 raw peanuts and 2 chana, soaked overnight
1 maize kernel, soaked overnight (optional)
a magnifying glass, if you have one
paper and coloured pencils

activities.safety: Use your fingernails to open the seeds. A grown-up cuts the maize kernel with a knife if you try one.

schedule.what: Soak the seeds the night before. Peel, split and look. Draw and label.

activities.record: Draw one opened bean, big. Label three parts: seed coat, baby plant and food store.

setup.art: A dry wrinkly rajma bean next to a fat smooth soaked one in a child's palm.
setup.caption: 1. Compare a dry bean with a soaked one.

setup.art: Fingers peeling the red coat off a soaked rajma, the creamy bean showing underneath.
setup.caption: 2. Rub off the coat. Gently split the bean in two along its edge.

setup.art: A magnifying glass over one half of a split bean, showing a tiny baby plant with a pointed root and two small folded leaves.
setup.caption: 3. Find the tiny baby plant at the edge. Draw it and label it.

flow.context: This is the first step of Open a Seed. You look inside soaked beans to find the baby plant.
flow.do: 1. Give your child one dry bean and one soaked bean. 2. Ask them to feel, look at and compare the two.
flow.say: This one has been in water all night. This one is dry. What is different?
flow.kid: Hold a dry bean and a soaked bean. Feel them. Look closely. What is different?

ask.q: What has the water done to the bean?
good: The skin is smooth and looser.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the pale scar on the side of the soaked bean. 2. Rub the coat until it slips off. 3. Gently split the bean along its edge into two halves with a fingernail.
flow.say: This little scar is where the bean was joined to its pod. Water got in near here. Now let's take off its coat and open it like a book.
flow.kid: Find the small pale scar on the bean. Rub off the coat. Use your nail to open the bean in two, like a book.
flow.parent: The scar is called the hilum. Splitting is easiest along the curved edge, opposite the scar side. Some halves will break. That is fine. Try another bean.

flow.do: 1. Look at the inside edge of one half, near the scar end. Use the magnifying glass. 2. Find the tiny baby plant, with a little pointed root and two tiny folded leaves. 3. Do the same with a peanut and a chana.
flow.say: Look near the end. Can you see a tiny plant? It has a little root and two tiny leaves, folded up. What do you think the two big halves are for?
flow.kid: Look near the end of one half. Find a tiny plant. It has a little root and two tiny leaves. What are the big halves for?
flow.parent: In a peanut, the baby plant is very easy to see at the pointed tip, between the halves. In maize there is only one food store, with a small pale patch on one face where the baby plant lies.

check.q: You split a soaked bean into its two big halves. What are those two halves for?
options: They are the food store that feeds the baby plant
check.why: The two big halves are seed leaves packed with food. They feed the baby plant until it can make food from sunlight. Picking 'shell' usually mixes up the halves with the thin coat, which you peeled off first. The roots have not grown yet. Only a tiny root tip is there, on the baby plant.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw one opened bean, big, and label the seed coat, the baby plant and the food store.
flow.say: Draw it as big as you can. Label three parts: the coat, the baby plant and its food store.
flow.kid: Draw your bean, big. Label the coat, the baby plant and the food store.
flow.think: The baby plant was already there before you soaked it. Who made it?

activities.title: Can Dal Sprout? Whole seeds against split and roasted ones
activities.context: This is a test with kitchen seeds. You put whole moong, split moong dal, raw peanuts and roasted peanuts on a wet cloth, and find out which can still sprout.

materials.item: 10 whole moong and 10 pieces of split moong dal
5 raw peanuts and 5 roasted peanuts, all soaked overnight with the moong
a plate, a wet cloth or tissue, and 4 paper labels

activities.safety: Do not eat the seeds after the test.

schedule.what: Soak the four groups the night before. Set them out on a wet cloth. Guess which will sprout.
Count which sprouted. Explain why.

activities.record: Write how many of each group sprouted.

setup.art: A plate with a wet cloth and four small groups: green whole moong, yellow split dal, pink-skinned raw peanuts and brown roasted peanuts, each with a paper label.
setup.caption: 1. Put four groups on a wet cloth, with labels.

setup.art: The same plate covered with another plate on a kitchen shelf.
setup.caption: 2. Cover the plate. Keep the cloth wet for 2 days.

setup.art: The plate two days later: the whole moong and raw peanuts with white tails, the dal and roasted peanuts unchanged.
setup.caption: 3. Count which ones sprouted.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Can Dal Sprout? test. You compare whole seeds with split and roasted ones.
flow.do: 1. The night before, soak all four groups in separate bowls of water. 2. In the morning, drain them and lay a wet cloth on a plate. 3. Put the four groups on it: whole moong, split moong dal, raw peanuts and roasted peanuts. 4. Label each group.
flow.say: These are the same kinds of seeds. Some are whole, some are split, and some are roasted. Which ones can still sprout?
flow.kid: Soak the four groups overnight. Put them on a wet cloth. Label them. Which ones will sprout? Guess first, and say why.

flow.do: 1. Cover the plate with another plate. 2. Keep the cloth wet. 3. After 2 days, count the sprouts in each group.
flow.say: Let's count. Which groups sprouted?
flow.kid: Cover the plate. Keep the cloth wet. After 2 days, count the sprouts in each group.
flow.parent: Moong sprouts in a day or two. Raw peanuts can take 2 to 4 days, so look again on day 4 if they have not started. In cold weather, keep the plate in the warmest place you have and allow a day or two more.

flow.do: Talk about why. Then ask your child to say what they think, what they saw and why.
flow.say: The dal and the roasted peanuts had water, warmth and air. So why didn't they sprout?
flow.kid: The dal had water, warmth and air. Why didn't it sprout? Say what you think, what you saw and why.
flow.parent: Split dal has lost its coat and has been split. The tiny baby plant is usually broken off. Roasting cooks the baby plant, so it is dead. A good answer: what I think, a seed needs a living baby plant to sprout. What I saw, 9 whole moong sprouted but no dal, and the raw peanuts sprouted but not the roasted ones. Why, the dal had lost its baby plant, and roasting killed the peanut's baby plant.

check.q: In the Can Dal Sprout? test, the roasted peanuts got water, warmth and air but did not sprout. Why?
options: Roasting killed the baby plant inside
check.why: Water, warmth and air only wake a seed that is alive. Roasting cooks the baby plant, so there is nothing left to wake. Picking 'more water' means thinking water alone makes seeds grow. Picking 'never sprout' is ruled out by the raw peanuts, which did sprout.

activities.title: The Seed Window: which way does the root grow?
activities.context: This is a jar where you can watch seeds sprout. You push soaked chana between wet paper and the glass, some upside down, and see which way the roots and shoots grow.

materials.item: a clear plastic jar with a lid, such as an empty pickle or sweets jar, or a tall clear cup with a plastic bag to cover it
paper towel or blotting paper
4 chana or rajma, soaked overnight
water

activities.safety: Use a plastic jar if you have one, so nothing breaks.

schedule.what: Set up the jar with seeds lying in different ways.
Look and draw. When roots are 2 cm long, pour out the water, close the jar and lay it on its side.
Look and draw again. Which way did the roots turn?

activities.record: Draw the seeds on day 1, day 3 and day 5. Draw an arrow showing which way each root grew.

setup.art: A clear jar lined with paper towel, four soaked chana pushed between the paper and the side halfway up, each pointing a different way, a little water at the bottom.
setup.caption: 1. Line a jar with paper. Push 4 seeds between paper and plastic, each a different way.

setup.art: The jar on day 3: every seed has a root, and every root is curving downwards.
setup.caption: 2. Watch the roots. They all turn to grow down.

setup.art: The jar laid on its side, the roots' tips bending to point down again.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the jar on its side. Watch the root tips bend down again.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Seed Window. You set up a jar so you can watch roots grow.
flow.do: 1. Line the inside of the jar with paper towel. 2. Push 4 soaked chana between the paper and the side, halfway up. 3. Put one scar up, one scar down, one on its side and one at a slant. 4. Pour about 2 cm of water in the bottom, so the paper stays wet.
flow.say: We've put the seeds every which way. When the roots come out, which way will they go?
flow.kid: Line a jar with paper. Push 4 seeds between the paper and the side. Put each one a different way. Add a little water at the bottom.

ask.q: Which will come out first, the root or the shoot?
good: The root, so it can drink and hold on.

flow.do: 1. After 2 days, look and draw each seed. 2. When the roots are about 2 cm long, pour out the water at the bottom. 3. Close the lid, or cover the cup with a plastic bag, so the paper stays wet. 4. Lay the jar on its side.
flow.say: Every root is going down, even the one that started pointing up. How does it know?
flow.kid: Look at the roots. Which way are they growing? Draw them. Pour out the water. Close the jar. Lay it on its side.

check.q: In the seed window jar, one chana was put in upside down. Which way does its root grow?
options: Up, the way it was pointing
check.why: Roots feel gravity and turn to grow down, whichever way the seed lies. Picking 'up' means thinking the root simply carries on the way the seed points. Watch: an upside-down seed's root curls round and heads down.

flow.parent: Chana roots usually show in 1 to 2 days in warm weather, and 3 to 4 days in a cold room. Wait until they are about 2 cm long before you turn the jar.

flow.do: After 2 more days, look again. Ask your child to say what they think, what they saw and why.
flow.say: We turned the jar. What did the root tips do?
flow.kid: What did the root tips do after you turned the jar? Say what you think, what you saw and why.
flow.parent: The root tips bend to point down again. Root tips have cells with tiny heavy grains of starch inside. The grains settle to the bottom, so the root can tell which way is down. A good answer: what I think, roots always grow down. What I saw, all 4 roots grew down, and when we turned the jar, they bent down again. Why, roots feel gravity.
flow.think: Astronauts have grown plants in space. Which way do you think their roots grew?

activities.title: Sweet Sprouts: a taste test
activities.context: This is a taste test. You chew a soaked moong seed and a two-day-old moong sprout, and find out which tastes sweeter.

materials.item: a few moong seeds soaked overnight, and a few that have sprouted for 2 days, both washed well
a glass of water to rinse your mouth

activities.safety: Use moong from the kitchen, washed in clean water, not seeds from a test. A grown-up can steam them for a minute first if your family prefers.

schedule.what: Soak a spoonful of moong overnight, then drain it and keep it damp in a cloth so it sprouts.
In the evening, soak a second spoonful of moong.
Taste a soaked seed and a two-day sprout. Compare.

activities.record: Write which tasted sweeter, and one word for each taste.

setup.art: Two small steel bowls, one with plain soaked moong and one with moong sprouts with white tails.
setup.caption: 1. Put soaked moong in one bowl and 2-day sprouts in another.

setup.art: A child with closed eyes slowly chewing, a glass of water beside them.
setup.caption: 2. Chew one of each slowly. Rinse your mouth in between.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Sweet Sprouts taste test. You compare a soaked seed with a sprouted one.
flow.do: 1. Ask your child to chew one soaked seed slowly, for 20 seconds. 2. Rinse with water. 3. Then chew one sprout slowly.
flow.say: Chew slowly and think about the taste. Is one of them sweeter?
flow.kid: Chew a soaked seed slowly. Sip water. Now chew a sprout slowly. Which is sweeter?

flow.do: Talk about why the sprout might taste sweeter.
flow.say: The seed's stored food is mostly starch. Starch is not sweet. But as it sprouts, the seed turns some starch into sugar. Why would it do that?
flow.kid: The seed's food is starch. Starch is not sweet. A sprout turns some starch into sugar. Why?
flow.parent: The baby plant cannot use starch directly. Enzymes, helpers made by its cells, cut starch into sugar that can travel to the growing root and shoot. The change is small, so not everyone can taste it. That is fine. Ragi malt is made from sprouted ragi for the same reason.

ask.q: Why does a sprouting seed turn starch into sugar?
good: So the baby plant can use it as food.
Sugar can move to the root and shoot.

activities.title: Be a Seed: act out sprouting
activities.context: This is a movement game. Children act out a seed waking up: drinking, swelling, pushing out a root, and lifting a shoot to the light.

materials.item: a clear space on the floor and, if you like, some slow music

activities.safety: Clear the space of anything hard or sharp.

schedule.what: Act out a seed sprouting, twice, slowly.

activities.record: Draw yourself as a sprouting seed, with your root and shoot.

setup.art: A child curled up tight on the floor like a seed, arms around knees.
setup.caption: 1. Curl up small and still, like a dry seed.

setup.art: The child stretching one leg out along the floor like a root, while still curled.
setup.caption: 2. Drink, swell, then push one leg out and down as your root.

setup.art: The child rising slowly with back bent like a hook, then straightening with arms open like two leaves.
setup.caption: 3. Rise with a bent back like a hook. Then open your arms like leaves.

flow.context: This is the first step of Be a Seed. You act out how a seed sprouts.
flow.do: Read out each stage slowly while your child acts it: dry seed, rain, swelling, root, hook, leaves.
flow.say: You are a dry seed, curled up and still. Now the rain comes. Drink it in. Swell bigger. Your coat splits. Push your root out first, down into the ground. Now your shoot. Rise slowly, with your back bent like a hook. Now straighten up, and open your two leaves to the sun.
flow.kid: Curl up tight. You are a dry seed. Rain! Drink it. Swell. Push your root out, down. Now rise slowly, bent like a hook. Stand up. Open your leaves.
flow.parent: Go slowly. Point out the order. The root comes first, then the shoot. The bent hook protects the shoot's soft tip as it pushes through the soil.

flow.do: Do it again, but this time call out a problem halfway, and let your child show what happens.
flow.say: Let's do it again. But this time, oh no, the cup is full of water. There is no air. What does the seed do?
flow.kid: Again! But this time a grown-up calls out a problem. Show what happens to the seed.
flow.parent: Problems to call out: no water (stay curled), a cold fridge (move very, very slowly), drowned with no air (stop and go floppy), a dark cupboard (keep going, because seeds can sprout in the dark).

check.q: In Be a Seed, which part of the seed comes out first?
check.why: The root comes out first, so the seedling can hold on and drink. Picking 'shoot' or 'leaves' is a common guess, because those are the parts we see first above the soil. Underground, the root was there before them.

activities.title: The Kitchen Seed Hunt
activities.context: This is a hunt in your kitchen. You find as many seeds as you can, line them up from smallest to biggest, and name the plant each one comes from.

materials.item: small amounts of seeds from the kitchen, such as rai, jeera, methi, sesame, moong, chana, rajma, peanuts, rice, a tamarind seed and a mango or jamun stone
a long strip of paper and a pencil

activities.safety: Ask before opening jars. Put everything back.

schedule.what: Hunt for seeds. Line them up. Name the plants.

activities.record: Make a line of seeds on the paper strip, from smallest to biggest. Write or draw the plant beside each one.

setup.art: A child at an open kitchen shelf of steel jars, holding a pinch of rai seeds.
setup.caption: 1. Find as many seeds as you can in the kitchen.

setup.art: A long paper strip on the floor with seeds lined up from a tiny rai grain to a big mango stone, small plant drawings beside each.
setup.caption: 2. Line them up, smallest to biggest. Name each plant.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Kitchen Seed Hunt. You look for seeds in your kitchen.
flow.do: Help your child find seeds in the kitchen. Take a few of each.
flow.say: Our kitchen is full of sleeping baby plants. How many different kinds can we find?
flow.kid: Your kitchen is full of seeds. How many kinds can you find? Take a few of each.
flow.parent: Good finds: rai, jeera, methi, sesame, ajwain, saunf, moong, masoor, chana, rajma, peanuts, rice, wheat, corn, cashew, a tamarind seed, a mango stone, seeds inside a tomato, a chilli or a papaya. Jeera, saunf and ajwain are really tiny dry fruits, each holding seeds.

flow.do: 1. Line them up on the paper strip from smallest to biggest. 2. Next to each, write or draw the plant it grows into.
flow.say: Does the biggest seed grow into the biggest plant?
flow.kid: Line them up, smallest to biggest. Draw the plant for each one. Does a big seed make a big plant?
flow.think: A banyan tree's seed is smaller than a rai grain. How does a giant tree come from something so small?

projects.title: My Seed Friend: a sprouting diary
projects.context: This is a 10-day project. You plant a rajma bean against the side of a clear cup, give it a name, look after it and draw it every day, from seed to its first true leaves.

materials.item: a clear plastic cup
soil from a potted plant, or cocopeat from a plant nursery
2 rajma beans, soaked overnight. Whole moong also works and grows faster. Do not use chana here, because its seed halves stay under the soil.
a ruler with millimetre marks, such as a school ruler
a notebook for the diary

projects.safety: Wash your hands after touching soil.

schedule.what: Plant two beans against the side of the cup. Name your seed friend. Draw it.
Water a little. Look through the side. Draw.
Look for the root. Measure it. Draw.
Water. Measure the root. Draw.
Look for the hooked shoot. Measure the root and the shoot. Draw.
Water. Measure. Draw.
Watch the seed halves lift and turn green. Measure. Draw.
Water. Measure. Draw.
Look for the first true leaves. Measure. Draw.
Make a growth table. Read your diary aloud to someone. Plant your friend in a bigger pot.

projects.record: A diary page for every day: a drawing, the root length and the shoot length in millimetres, and one sentence.

setup.art: A clear plastic cup filled with soil, two soaked beans pressed against the inside wall so they can be seen from outside.
setup.caption: 1. Push two soaked beans into soil against the side of a clear cup.

setup.art: A child writing a name label, 'Raju', and sticking it on the cup.
setup.caption: 2. Give your seed friend a name.

setup.art: The cup a week later, with a white root visible down the side and a green shoot with two leaves above the soil, a ruler beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Every day, look, measure and draw in your diary.

flow.context: This is the first step of My Seed Friend. You plant a bean where you can watch it sprout, and start a diary.
flow.do: 1. Fill the cup with damp soil. 2. Push two soaked beans down against the side, about 2 cm deep, so you can see them through the plastic. 3. Name the plant. 4. Draw it on page 1 of the diary.
flow.say: This is your seed friend. You will look after it, and it will show you how it grows. What will you call it?
flow.kid: Fill the cup with damp soil. Push two beans against the side, so you can see them. Give your seed friend a name. Draw it.
flow.parent: Two beans are planted in case one does not sprout. Kitchen rajma is sometimes old, so if neither sprouts in 5 days, try two fresh ones. Keep the cup out of hot direct sun for the first days, but in a bright place once the shoot is up. The soil should be damp, never soggy.

flow.do: Each day: 1. Water a little if the top of the soil is dry. 2. Look through the side. 3. Measure the root and, later, the shoot in millimetres. 4. Draw and write one sentence.
flow.say: What has changed since yesterday? Measure it.
flow.kid: Each day, look at your seed friend. Water a little if the soil is dry. Measure the root and the shoot. Draw it. Write one sentence.
flow.parent: In warm weather, the root usually shows by day 2 or 3, and the hooked shoot comes up by day 4 to 6. The seed halves, the seed leaves, lift up and turn green, then shrink as their food is used up. The first true leaves open by about day 8 to 10. In a cold room everything takes a few days longer, so keep the cup in the warmest bright place you have.

check.q: In your seed diary, the two fat seed halves of the bean lifted up, turned green, then got smaller. Why did they shrink?
options: The baby plant used up their stored food
check.why: The seed halves are the food store. As the plant grows, it uses their food, so they shrink. Once its true leaves can make food from sunlight, it does not need them any more. Picking 'dried in the sun' is a fair guess, but they shrink even in the shade.

flow.do: If your seed friend dies, write a short note about how you feel. Talk about what might have gone wrong: too much water, too little, too cold, or no air in soggy soil. Plant the second bean.
flow.say: Sometimes a seed friend doesn't make it. That is sad, and it's all right to feel sad. What do you think it needed?
flow.kid: Did your seed friend die? That is sad. Write a short note about how you feel. What do you think it needed? Try again with the second bean.
flow.parent: This step is only needed if the plant dies. It comes from the founder's idea of writing a mourning note for a plant that could not be saved.

flow.do: On day 10, put the root and shoot lengths into a table. Read the diary aloud to someone. Move the plant to a bigger pot.
flow.say: Read your diary to someone in the family. What surprised you most?
flow.kid: Make a table of your measurements. Read your diary to someone. What surprised you most? Plant your friend in a bigger pot.
flow.think: Your bean has used up the food in its seed halves. Where will it get its food now?

challenges.title: Fastest Sprouts
challenges.problem: Your family wants moong sprouts for breakfast as soon as possible. Your job is to get 20 moong seeds to grow roots at least 1 cm long, in the shortest time.
constraints: Use only 20 moong seeds from the same packet.
No stove, oven or heater. You may use only safe warm places, like a kitchen shelf.
Write down the time you start and the time 15 of the 20 seeds have roots 1 cm long.
materials: a cloth, a strainer, cups, cotton or a tiffin
general: Soak the seeds for about 8 to 12 hours. Then drain them, so they have water and air.
Keep them damp, not under water. Rinse them once or twice a day, so they don't go sour.
Keep them in a warm spot, like a kitchen shelf, out of hot sun. Light is not needed.
creative: Hang them in a loose cloth bundle, the way many families do, so air reaches every seed.
Put them in a strainer over a bowl, covered with a damp cloth, so extra water drips away.
Some families wrap the bundle and keep it in a warm closed casserole. Does keeping in the warmth beat letting in more air?
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own way. Draw it, try it and time it. Did you beat the usual way?

setup.art: A bowl of moong soaking in water beside a clock showing 8 o'clock.
setup.caption: 1. Soak 20 moong seeds. Write the start time.

setup.art: Three ways side by side: a loose hanging cloth bundle, a strainer over a bowl covered with a damp cloth, and a closed casserole.
setup.caption: 2. Try your sprouting ideas: water, warmth and air.

setup.art: A ruler next to moong sprouts with roots 1 cm long, a clock showing the time.
setup.caption: 3. Check the roots. Write the time when 15 seeds have 1 cm roots.

flow.context: This is the first step of Fastest Sprouts. It is a challenge to sprout moong as fast as you can, using what you know about water, warmth and air.
flow.do: Before soaking anything, list three ideas together for making the seeds sprout faster.
flow.say: Remember what a seed needs: water, warmth and air. How can we give it all three, as well as possible?
flow.kid: Think like a scientist. A seed needs water, warmth and air. Draw or write three ideas to make it sprout faster.

flow.wait: Check every few hours for 2 days
flow.do: 1. Try your best idea with the 20 seeds. 2. Check every few hours, when you can. 3. Write down the time when 15 of the seeds have roots 1 cm long.
flow.say: Let's check. How many have 1 cm roots yet?
flow.kid: Try your best idea. Check every few hours. When do 15 seeds have roots 1 cm long? Write the time.
flow.parent: Moong usually takes about 1 to 2 days to reach 1 cm roots in warm weather, and 3 days or more in a cold room. Warmth speeds it up. Too much water slows it down and makes it sour.

flow.do: Read the usual ways and the creative ideas together. Then invent a new way and try it next time.
flow.say: Here's what people usually do, and some creative ideas. Can you invent a way that beats them?
flow.kid: Look at the usual ways and the creative ideas. Now invent your own way. Can you beat them?
flow.think: Farmers who sprout paddy seed before sowing keep it in wet sacks. Why sacks, and not sealed tins?

challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You must get 20 moong seeds to sprout as fast as possible, by giving them water, warmth and air.

challenges.title: Seeds for the Moon Base
challenges.problem: Astronauts are going to live on the Moon. They will take seeds to grow food. Design a seed kit that keeps the seeds asleep for the journey, then wakes them on the Moon.
constraints: The Moon has no air to breathe and no liquid water. Its nights last about 14 Earth days and are colder than any freezer.
Your kit must keep the seeds safe and asleep on the trip, then give them what they need to sprout.
Build a model from things at home, and test the 'wake up' part with real moong seeds.
materials: a small plastic box or bottle with a lid
a cloth or a woollen sock for warmth
general: Keep the seeds dry and cool on the journey, so they stay asleep. That is how seed banks store them.
On the Moon, give them water, keep them warm and give them air, inside a sealed box or a base.
Use a light later, once the seedlings come up, because they will need it to make food.
creative: China's Chang'e 4 lander took cotton seeds to the Moon in 2019. A cotton seed sprouted, then died when the long lunar night froze it. How would your kit stay warm all night?
Could the astronauts' own breath give the seeds air? Could the seeds' breathing warm a little box?
Could the seeds travel with their own water sealed beside them, to be let in with a pull of a tab?
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own Moon seed kit. Draw it, build a model and test whether it wakes moong seeds on Earth.

setup.art: A child drawing a plan of a sealed seed box with compartments for dry seeds, water, air and a warm cover.
setup.caption: 1. Draw your Moon seed kit.

setup.art: A small plastic box with moong on cotton, a tiny water bottle beside it and a woollen sock wrapped around it.
setup.caption: 2. Build a model and add water, warmth and air.

setup.art: The box opened two days later with moong sprouts inside, the child holding it up.
setup.caption: 3. Test it. Did your seeds wake up?

flow.context: This is the first step of Seeds for the Moon Base. It is a design challenge: keep seeds asleep on the way to the Moon, then wake them up there.
flow.do: Read the problem together. List what the Moon is missing, and what a seed needs.
flow.say: A seed needs water, warmth and air. Which of those does the Moon have?
flow.kid: What does a seed need? What does the Moon not have? Make two lists.

flow.do: Draw a plan, then build a model kit from things at home. Put real moong inside for the wake-up test.
flow.say: Your kit has two jobs. It must keep the seeds asleep, then wake them. How will it do both?
flow.kid: Draw your kit. Then build it. Put real moong in it. Add water, warmth and air when it is time to wake them.

flow.do: After 2 days, open the kit. Count the sprouts. Read the usual ideas and the creative ones together.
flow.say: Did your seeds wake up? What would you change for the real Moon?
flow.kid: Open your kit. Did the seeds sprout? What would you change for the real Moon?
flow.think: Why do you think scientists send seeds to space at all?

challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You plan a kit that carries seeds to the Moon and helps them sprout there.
