opts: A baby plant and its food store
quiz.why: Every seed holds a living baby plant and a store of food for it. Picking 'nothing' is an easy mistake, because the baby plant is tiny. Soak a bean, split it and look closely. It is there.

quiz.p: What are the two big halves of a split chana?
opts: The food store, in its two seed leaves
quiz.why: They are seed leaves packed with food. The thin seed coat is outside them, and the tiny baby plant sits between them. Picking 'two baby plants' mixes up the food store with the plant it feeds.

quiz.p: Which three things do most seeds need to sprout?
quiz.why: Water wakes the seed, warmth makes it work faster and air lets it breathe. Picking 'sunlight and soil' is the most common mistake. A seed carries its own food.

quiz.p: Does a moong seed need light to sprout?
opts: No, it sprouts in the dark too
Yes, it can't sprout without light
quiz.why: Moong sprouts in a dark tiffin. Grown plants need light, which is why many people guess 'yes'. A few tiny seeds, like some lettuce, do need light. Moong does not.

quiz.p: In the five-cup test, you put 10 moong seeds in each of 5 cups: dry, damp, damp in the fridge, under water with oil on top, and damp in the light. Which cup tests whether seeds need warmth?
quiz.why: The fridge cup has water and air, but is cold. So it tests warmth. Picking the dry cup mixes up warmth and water.
quiz.context: In the five-cup test, you put 10 moong seeds in each of 5 cups: dry, damp, damp in the fridge, under water with oil on top, and damp in the light.

quiz.p: Why must a fair test change only one thing?
opts: So we know which thing made the difference
quiz.why: If we changed two things at once, we would not know which one caused the result. Picking 'quicker' misses the point. Fair tests are about trusting the answer.

quiz.p: In the five-cup test, you put 10 moong seeds in each of 5 cups: dry, damp, damp in the fridge, under water with oil on top, and damp in the light. Look at the chart. How many more seeds sprouted in the damp warm cup than in the fridge cup?
quiz.why: The damp, warm cup had 9 and the fridge cup had 1. 9 take away 1 is 8. Picking 9 means reading just the damp cup's bar, not the difference.
quiz.context: In the five-cup test, you put 10 moong seeds in each of 5 cups: dry, damp, damp in the fridge, under water with oil on top, and damp in the light.

chart.title: Made-up example: seeds sprouted out of 10, after 3 days

quiz.p: You soaked moong at 8 o'clock in the evening. The first roots appeared at 8 o'clock the next evening. How long did that take?
quiz.why: From 8 in the evening to 8 the next evening is a full day, 24 hours. Picking 12 hours means counting only from evening to morning.

quiz.p: A cloth bundle of sprouting moong feels warm in the middle. Why?
opts: The seeds are breathing, which makes warmth
quiz.why: Sprouting seeds use oxygen to get energy from their stored food. Some energy comes out as warmth. A boiled seed is dead and makes no warmth.

quiz.p: Why do seeds sealed under water often go sour and fail to sprout?
opts: They cannot get enough air to breathe
quiz.why: Water holds only a little oxygen. Seeds sealed under it cannot breathe well, so they fail and go sour. Picking 'poisonous' is wrong. Seeds need water, just not too much of it.

quiz.p: What happens to a seed's food store as the seedling grows?
opts: It gets used up, so the seed halves shrink
quiz.why: The baby plant lives on its stored food until its green leaves can make food. So the seed halves shrink. Picking 'grows bigger' is a natural guess, but the food is being eaten, not made.

quiz.p: What is the first thing that happens when a dry seed gets wet?
quiz.why: The seed soaks up water and swells, often to about twice its weight. Then its coat splits and the root comes out.

quiz.p: A seed is planted upside down. Which way will its root grow?
opts: Up, the way the seed was pointing
quiz.why: Root tips feel gravity, so roots always turn to grow down. Picking 'up' means thinking the root just follows the way the seed points.

quiz.p: How long can a seed stay alive?
opts: It depends on the seed. Some last a year or two, and a few have sprouted after hundreds of years. Nobody knows the limit.
quiz.why: A date palm seed about 2,000 years old sprouted in 2005. Most seeds last far less. Scientists still do not know the longest a seed can live.

quiz.p: Do scientists agree that a dry seed is alive?
opts: Most say yes, alive but asleep. Some say life almost stops in it, and philosophers still argue about what 'alive' means.
Yes, and there is nothing more to say
No, everyone agrees it is dead
quiz.why: Most biologists call a dry seed dormant: alive, but asleep. Because it does so little, some scientists and thinkers say it sits between alive and not alive. This is still discussed.

Sprouts of moong, chana and methi are sold in markets and eaten in usal, salads and chaat.
Malt, made by sprouting grains like barley and ragi, is used in ragi malt, some sweets, bread and drinks.

Gardeners soak hard seeds like bhindi and bitter gourd overnight, so water gets in faster.
Gardeners nick or rub very hard seeds with sandpaper to let water in.

Space agencies test seeds in space, to plan how astronauts could grow food on the Moon and Mars.
Forest workers collect and sprout seeds of native trees to plant new forests.
Seed balls, seeds rolled into balls of clay and soil, are thrown onto bare land so they sprout when rain comes.

open_questions.q: How long can a seed stay alive?
open_questions.why_open: Some have sprouted after 2,000 years. Nobody knows the real limit, and it is different for every kind of seed. Experiments like Beal's bottles take centuries.

open_questions.q: How does a seed decide when to wake?
open_questions.why_open: Seeds sense water, warmth, light and some chemicals. How they add all these signals together is still being worked out.

open_questions.q: Why do some seeds of the same plant wake at once, and others wait for years?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists think it spreads the risk, like not putting all your eggs in one basket. How each seed is set to wait is not fully known.

open_questions.q: How do seeds repair the damage of getting old while they sleep?
open_questions.why_open: Seeds have repair tools for their cells. Scientists are still finding out how they work, and why some seeds are so much better at it.

open_questions.q: Can we store seeds that do not like being dried, like mango, jackfruit and many rainforest seeds?
open_questions.why_open: These seeds die if dried or frozen, so normal seed banks cannot keep them. Scientists are testing new ways, such as freezing just the baby plant in liquid nitrogen.

open_questions.q: Could we grow crops from seed on the Moon or Mars?
open_questions.why_open: Seeds have sprouted on the Moon in a sealed box and in Moon soil brought to Earth. Growing whole crops there, through many generations, has never been done.

open_questions.q: Is a dry seed alive, or something in between?
open_questions.why_open: It depends on what we mean by 'alive'. Scientists and philosophers still discuss it.

maths.problem: Look at the chart from the five-cup test. How many seeds sprouted in all five cups together? And how many seeds did not sprout?
maths.explain: Add the bars: 0 + 9 + 1 + 2 + 9 = 21 seeds sprouted. There were 10 seeds in each of 5 cups, so 50 seeds in all. 50 take away 21 is 29. So 29 seeds did not sprout.
maths.context: This is about the five-cup test. You put 10 moong seeds in each of 5 cups: dry, damp, damp in the fridge, under water with oil, and damp in the light. After 3 days you counted the seeds with roots.

chart.title: Made-up example: how many of 10 moong seeds sprouted in 3 days
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

maths.why_maths: A bar chart lets you read every cup's result at a glance. Adding the bars tells you about the whole test, not just one cup.

maths.problem: In the damp, warm cup, 9 out of 10 seeds sprouted. In a bigger test, a farmer sows 100 seeds of the same kind in the same way. About how many would you expect to sprout?
maths.explain: 9 out of every 10 sprouted. 100 seeds is 10 lots of 10. So expect 10 lots of 9 sprouts. 10 times 9 is 90. It may not be exactly 90, because every seed is a little different.
maths.context: This is about the five-cup test, where you counted how many of 10 moong seeds sprouted in each cup.
maths.why_maths: Farmers need to know how many seeds to sow. Scaling up from a small test of 10 seeds tells them how many plants to expect in a field.

maths.problem: In the swelling test, 50 grams of dry chana weighed 100 grams after soaking overnight. How many grams of water did the chana drink? How many times heavier was it?
maths.answer: 50 grams of water. It was 2 times as heavy.
maths.explain: 100 grams take away 50 grams is 50 grams. That is the water inside the seeds. 50 + 50 = 100, so the soaked chana weighs 2 lots of 50 grams. It is 2 times as heavy.
maths.context: This is about the swelling test. You weighed some dry chana, soaked it overnight, patted it dry and weighed it again.

chart.title: Weight of the chana before and after soaking

maths.why_maths: Weighing turns 'the seeds got bigger' into an exact answer: how much water a seed drinks before it can sprout.

maths.problem: The thermometer in the flask of live sprouts shows 31 degrees Celsius. The flask of boiled seeds shows 27 degrees. How much warmer are the live sprouts?
maths.explain: 31 take away 27 is 4. So the live sprouts are 4 degrees Celsius warmer. Count up from 27 to check: 28, 29, 30, 31. That is 4 steps.
maths.context: This is about the warm flask test. You put live sprouting moong in one flask and boiled moong in another, with a thermometer in each.

chart.title: The thermometer in the live sprouts flask (degrees Celsius)
chart.label: Each mark is 1 degree.

maths.why_maths: The warmth from breathing seeds is small. Reading a thermometer and finding the difference shows it clearly, as a number.

maths.problem: In your seed diary, the root of your bean was 6 millimetres on day 3, 15 millimetres on day 4 and 27 millimetres on day 5. How much did it grow each day? Did it grow faster or slower as the days went on?
maths.answer: 9 millimetres from day 3 to day 4, then 12 millimetres from day 4 to day 5. It grew faster.
maths.explain: 15 take away 6 is 9. So it grew 9 millimetres on the first day. 27 take away 15 is 12. So it grew 12 millimetres on the next day. 12 is more than 9, so the root was growing faster.
maths.context: This is about the seed diary project. You planted a bean against the side of a clear cup and measured its root every day.

chart.title: Made-up example: root length in the seed diary

maths.why_maths: Taking yesterday's length from today's tells you how fast the root is growing, not just how long it is.

maths.problem: You soaked moong at 7 o'clock in the evening. You drained it at 7 o'clock the next morning. The first roots showed at 7 o'clock that evening. How long did the seeds soak? How long from soaking to the first roots?
maths.answer: They soaked for 12 hours. From soaking to the first roots took 24 hours.
maths.explain: From 7 in the evening to 7 in the morning is 12 hours. From 7 in the morning to 7 in the evening is another 12 hours. 12 + 12 = 24 hours, which is one whole day.
maths.context: This is about making moong sprouts at home, the way Noor's mother did in the story: soak overnight, drain in the morning, and wait for the roots.
maths.why_maths: Sprouting takes time. Working out how many hours it takes helps you plan, so the sprouts are ready for breakfast.

roots.context: We have been learning how a seed wakes up and lives on its stored food. Now we ask what a sprout tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: A sprout in the dark grows longer each day, yet dried out, it weighs less than the seed did. It builds its root and shoot from the food its parent packed, and breathes some of it away. That breathing is what warmed the flask of sprouts. So a seedling's first growth is a race to reach light before its stored food runs out.
deep_truth.habit: We think growing always means gaining, getting heavier by taking more in. A seedling in the dark grows by spending what it carries, and only later starts to earn its own food from sunlight.
deep_truth.evidence: The flask of live sprouts warmed up, while boiled seeds did not, because the sprouts were breathing away their stored food. The rajma's seed halves shrank as the seedling grew. Sprouts kept in the dark for a week and then dried weigh less than the same number of dry seeds.

three.who_am_i: Before you could find food yourself, you grew on food your mother's body gave you. A seed starts the same way, on food from its parent.
three.what_is_life: Life can wait, and then it can spend. A seed rests for years, then uses its stored food fast to reach the light.
three.what_is_this_world: A sprout runs on sunlight that fell on its parent's leaves months ago. The Sun's energy is passed on from plant to plant.

roots.thread: A seed's food was made by its parent from air, water and sunlight. The sprout breathes that food back into the air as it grows. Then its own green leaves catch new sunlight and make food for the seeds it will one day pack. So the same sunlight and the same carbon keep passing from plant to air to plant. DeepKids believes that one awareness runs through this whole chain, and that the seed is aware in its own way: its root senses which way is down and chooses where to grow.

teachings.teaching: A father, Uddalaka, asks his son Shvetaketu to split a banyan seed. 'What do you see?' 'Nothing at all.' The father says: from this finest thing that you cannot see, the great banyan tree grows. That fine essence is in everything. And you are that.
teachings.link: When you split a bean, the baby plant is so small you can hardly see it, yet a whole plant grows from it. Uddalaka used a seed to show that what we cannot see can hold something great. A sprout grows big from a tiny start, fed by what was packed inside it.

teachings.teaching: A farmer from the state of Song was worried his young plants were growing too slowly. So he pulled on each one to help it grow. When his son ran to look, the plants had all withered.
teachings.link: You cannot make a seed sprout by pushing it. You can only give it water, warmth and air, and wait. Growing has its own time.

science.text: Seedlings grown in the dark get longer but lose dry weight, because breathing uses up their stored food. Plant scientists have measured this for well over a hundred years.
A dry seed's cells are not dead. They are still whole, with their repair tools ready, and breathe at a tiny rate. Exactly how close to 'stopped' life can get, and still restart, is being studied.

other_view.view: A seed's stored food is fuel, a bit like the fuel in a scooter's tank. Using it up is chemistry and timing. They see no need for a shared awareness to explain it, and that is an honest view.

how_we_found_out.context: Why does a root always grow down? This card tells the true story of how scientists found out.
how_we_found_out.story: People once thought a root grows down simply because it is looking for soil and water. In 1806, an English gardener and scientist, Thomas Andrew Knight, tested this. He fixed sprouting bean seeds around the rim of a wheel. Water from a stream kept the wheel spinning, day and night. A spinning wheel pushes things outwards, like the push you feel on a fast ride at a mela. If roots only followed water and soil, the spinning would not change them. Instead, every root grew outwards, in the direction of the push, and every shoot grew inwards. So a root grows the way a force pulls on it. On Earth, that force is gravity. In 1880, Charles Darwin and his son Francis cut the very tip off some growing roots. Those roots kept growing, but they no longer turned downwards. So the tip is the part that senses which way is down. In 1900, two scientists, Gottlieb Haberlandt and Bohumil Němec, each suggested how: tiny heavy grains of starch settle at the bottom of the root-tip cells.
how_we_found_out.who: Thomas Andrew Knight in England (1806); Charles and Francis Darwin in England (1880); Gottlieb Haberlandt and Bohumil Němec (1900)
how_we_found_out.when: The spinning wheel in 1806; the root-tip test in 1880; the starch grains suggested in 1900
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That roots grow down only because they are looking for soil and water. On Knight's spinning wheel, the roots grew outwards, the way the push went, even though the water and soil were the same all round.
how_we_found_out.art: A wooden wheel turned by a stream, with small bean seedlings fixed around its rim, every root pointing outwards and every shoot pointing in towards the centre.
